title: Your Body in One Level
objective: After this level you can name the body's main systems and what each one does.
summary: The body runs as 11 organ systems, each a team of organs with a big job: wrapping and moving, supplying and cleaning, controlling and defending. None works alone.

cards.headline: You're not one machine. You're a crew of 11.
cards.body: Anatomy textbooks split the body into 11 organ systems, each a group of organs sharing one big job. Here's the whole crew in one level, plus the rule they all live by: nobody works alone.

mascot.line: Eleven teams on one payroll, and you never have to schedule a single shift.

cards.headline: Eleven systems, three kinds of work

items.label: Wrap, hold up, move
points: Integumentary (skin, hair, nails): wraps you
Skeletal: the frame that holds you up
Muscular: moves you and helps keep you warm

items.label: Supply and clean up
points: Respiratory: oxygen in, carbon dioxide out
Digestive: processes food for the body to use
Cardiovascular (heart and vessels): delivers oxygen and nutrients
Urinary: filters waste from blood, balances water

items.label: Control, defend, continue
points: Nervous: senses and responds
Endocrine: sends hormones that regulate the body
Lymphatic: returns fluid, defends against germs
Reproductive: makes sex cells

cards.headline: One flight of stairs, five systems
cards.body: Climb some stairs and watch the crew. Your nervous system takes in where the steps are and sets off a response. Muscles pull on your skeleton to lift you. Meanwhile your respiratory system brings oxygen into your blood, and your cardiovascular system carries it to the muscles doing the work. One step, five systems, zero meetings.

cards.fact: Staying warm is a team job too.
cards.context: Your muscles help keep your body warm, and your cardiovascular system spreads that warmth around, evening out the temperature across your body. Neither system has 'heating' as its main job, yet between them they keep you at a steady temperature. Two systems, one thermostat.

cards.headline: Your body: mapped

Wrap and move, supply and clean, control and defend
Systems work as a team: lungs and heart share oxygen delivery
Muscles and circulation share keeping you warm

options.label: Leg muscles make their own oxygen

title: Cells
objective: After this level you can explain what a cell is and name its main parts.
summary: A cell is the basic building block of life. Its membrane controls what gets in and out, cytoplasm fills it, the nucleus gives orders and mitochondria supply energy.

cards.headline: An oak, a mushroom and you are built from the same kind of brick.
cards.body: It's the cell, the basic building block of every living thing. Your body is made of trillions of them. So what does one cell actually do, and what's inside it?

cards.headline: Every cell runs its own small life
cards.body: Each of your cells takes in nutrients from food, turns them into energy and does a special job, from giving your body structure to work that only its kind of cell can do. Cells also carry your hereditary material and can make copies of themselves. Trillions of small lives, all running at once, add up to one big one: yours.

cards.headline: A town with a wall
cards.body: Picture a cell as a tiny walled town. The plasma membrane is the wall: an outer lining that separates the cell from its surroundings and decides what gets in and out. Inside the wall is the cytoplasm, a jelly-like fluid packed with working parts. Everything the cell does happens inside that wall.

mascot.line: A walled town with its own power grid, and you have trillions of them. That is a lot of tiny mayors.

cards.headline: A town hall and power stations
cards.body: In the middle sits the nucleus, the command center. It sends out directions telling the cell when to grow, mature, divide or die. Out in the cytoplasm, mitochondria are the power stations: they turn energy from food into a form the cell can use. Orders from the hall, power from the stations: that's a working town.

cards.headline: Cells: opened
learned: Cells are the building blocks of all living things
The plasma membrane controls what gets in and out
The nucleus is the command center
Mitochondria turn food energy into usable energy

questions.prompt: Which part of a cell is its command center, telling it when to grow, divide or die?

options.label: They are the largest parts of the body

title: How Many Cells?
objective: After this level you can estimate how many cells make up a body and how many kinds there are.
summary: A 2016 estimate gives a reference adult about 30 trillion human cells, mostly red blood cells. Counts vary with body size, and the cells come in about 400 types.

cards.headline: Counting your cells at one per second would take about 950,000 years.
cards.body: No sleep, no snacks, no weekends off. Nobody has ever counted them one by one, of course. So how did scientists arrive at a number, and how many different kinds of cell are in the pile?

cards.fact: You're built from about 30 trillion human cells.
cards.context: That's the 2016 estimate by Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo, for a 'reference man': a young adult weighing 70 kg. They didn't count cells one at a time. They combined estimates for each cell type, like red blood cells and platelets, and added them up. Red blood cells alone made up about 84 percent of the total.

cards.headline: Your number depends on your body
cards.body: A 2023 study by Ian Hatton and colleagues ran the count for different bodies: about 36 trillion cells in a reference man, 28 trillion in a reference woman and 17 trillion in a 10-year-old child. A smaller body is built from fewer cells. So 'about 30 trillion' is a fair round figure for a grown-up. Think of it as a ballpark, not a barcode.

mascot.line: Same body, same team, and some players are a shrew while others are a whale.

cards.headline: About 400 kinds, from shrews to whales
cards.body: The same study sorted the body's cells into about 400 types, and their sizes are wildly different. From a tiny red blood cell to the biggest muscle fibers, cell mass spans about seven orders of magnitude, like going from a shrew to a blue whale. So red blood cells win the headcount, while muscle cells, few but huge, make up about half your cell mass.

title: From Cells to Organs
objective: After this level you can explain how cells form tissues, organs and whole systems.
summary: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form systems. The four tissue types are epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous, and the stomach wall uses all four.

cards.headline: Your stomach isn't made of 'stomach'.
cards.body: Its wall is a lining, packing, muscle and nerves: four different tissues stacked into one organ. Every organ is built from tissues like that. Here's the ladder from a single cell to a whole working body.

cards.headline: Cells, tissues, organs, systems, you
cards.body: Your body is built in levels. A tissue is a group of similar cells working together on one job. An organ is a distinct structure made of two or more tissue types. An organ system is a group of organs teaming up on a major job, and your 11 systems together make the whole organism: you. Each rung of the ladder is built from the one below it.

items.label: Cover and hold
points: Epithelial: sheets that cover surfaces and line passages
Connective: binds, supports and protects

items.label: Move and signal
points: Muscle: contracts to make movement
Nervous: sends signals between body parts

mascot.line: Lining, packing, muscle, wiring. Your stomach is basically a very well built lunchbox.

cards.headline: The stomach, layer by layer
cards.body: Back to that stomach. Inside is an epithelial lining. Around it, connective tissue holds the layers together. Then come three layers of smooth muscle that churn food, with networks of nerves running through the wall. Four tissue types, one organ, and that organ is one member of the digestive system you met in Level 1.

cards.headline: The ladder: climbed
learned: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs
Organs form organ systems

title: DNA, the Instruction Book
objective: After this level you can explain what DNA is and where the body keeps it.
summary: DNA is the hereditary instruction book, written in four letters (A, C, G, T). Nearly every cell keeps a copy, mostly in the nucleus, with a little in the mitochondria.

cards.headline: A single cell of yours holds about 2 meters of instructions.
cards.body: Stretch out the DNA from just one of your cells and it would reach about six feet. Yet it's packed into a nucleus so small you'd need a specialized microscope to see it. What is this stuff, and where exactly does your body keep it?

cards.headline: A four-letter alphabet
cards.body: DNA is your hereditary material: the instructions for building and running you. It's written in four chemical letters, A, C, G and T, and as with words in a sentence, the order carries the meaning. Your full set runs to about 3 billion letters, and more than 99 percent of them are the same in everyone. You and a stranger differ by a sliver.

cards.headline: Kept in the command center
cards.body: Nearly every cell in your body has the same DNA. Most of it sits in the nucleus, Level 2's command center, packaged into 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs. Its two strands twist into a double helix, a spiral ladder whose rungs are paired letters: A with T, C with G. A small amount of DNA also lives in the mitochondria, the cell's power stations.

mascot.line: Your body's most common cell, and it travels without the manual. Bold.

cards.fact: Your most common cell has no nucleus at all.
cards.context: Remember Level 3? Red blood cells make up about 84 percent of your cells. Mature ones have no nucleus, so they don't carry the nuclear instruction book. So when you read that 'nearly every cell' has your DNA, the 'nearly' is doing real work.

cards.headline: DNA: located
learned: DNA is the hereditary material
Four letters, about 3 billion of them, over 99% shared
Mostly in the nucleus, a little in mitochondria
Mature red blood cells have no nucleus

options.label: They share no DNA at all

options.label: They store it in their mitochondria

title: Genes
objective: After this level you can explain what a gene does and how genes lead to proteins.
summary: A gene is a stretch of DNA; about 20,000 of yours code for proteins. A cell copies a gene into messenger RNA, and a ribosome reads it to build a protein.

cards.headline: The recipes are kept in the nucleus. The kitchen is outside.
cards.body: Most of your DNA sits in the nucleus, but the machines that build proteins, called ribosomes, work out in the cytoplasm. So how does a recipe reach the kitchen? Follow one gene.

cards.headline: A gene is one recipe
cards.body: A gene is a stretch of DNA, the basic unit of heredity. Many genes are instructions for making a protein; many others act like switches that control other genes. You have about 20,000 protein-coding genes, and together they fill less than 2 percent of your DNA. If your DNA is a cookbook, a gene is one recipe.

cards.headline: Proteins do the work
cards.body: The dish is a protein, and proteins do most of the work in your cells. Some are enzymes that run chemical reactions, some carry messages between cells, and some give cells their structure. Each is a chain built from 20 kinds of amino acids, strung like pearls on a necklace. The order of the pearls sets the protein's shape, and the shape sets its job.

mascot.line: Photocopy the recipe, cook from the copy. Every good kitchen works that way.

cards.headline: From recipe to dish in two steps
cards.body: First, transcription: the cell copies a gene into messenger RNA, a working copy that carries the message out of the nucleus. Then translation: a ribosome in the cytoplasm reads that copy three letters at a time. Each three-letter codon usually calls for one amino acid, and the ribosome links them in order. The original recipe stays safely on the shelf.

cards.fact: A gene makes a protein, not a person.
cards.context: Most traits don't come down to one gene. Height, for example, is shaped by hundreds of gene variants, each with a small effect, plus things like nutrition. Genes supply the recipes; a whole body is more like a banquet.

title: Water and You
objective: After this level you can explain how much of the body is water and why that matters.
summary: Water is about 75% of a newborn and 50 to 60% of an adult, less with age or more body fat. Almost two-thirds of it sits inside cells, and it cools, cushions and cleans.

cards.headline: How much of you is water? It depends on your birthday.
cards.body: A newborn is about three-quarters water. Most adults are closer to half, or a bit more. No single number fits everyone. So where is all that water, and what is it doing?

cards.fact: Water is about 75% of a newborn, 50 to 60% of an adult, and less in old age.
cards.context: The share changes because the body's mix of tissues changes over a lifetime. Fat tissue holds less water than lean tissue, so people with more body fat have a lower percentage of water. Any single 'you are this much water' figure is a rough average at best.

cards.headline: Most of it is inside your cells
cards.body: Almost two-thirds of your body's water sits inside your cells, where it's the main ingredient of the jelly-like cytoplasm from Level 2. The rest is outside them, around your cells and in your blood. So don't picture a water tank. Picture trillions of tiny water-filled bags.

mascot.line: Coolant, cushion and cleaning crew, all in one liquid. Water does not like to specialize.

cards.headline: Water's day jobs
cards.body: All that water is busy. It helps keep your temperature normal: when you sweat, the evaporating water cools your skin. It lubricates and cushions your joints, protects your spinal cord and other sensitive tissues, and carries waste out of your body. Less a statue, more a fountain.

title: The Microbes on You
objective: After this level you can explain the trillions of microbes that live on and in the body.
summary: About 38 trillion bacteria, mostly in the colon, live alongside about 30 trillion human cells: roughly one to one. They weigh about 0.2 kg and help digest food.

cards.headline: Roughly half the cells in and on you aren't human.
cards.body: They're bacteria, and most of them live in your gut. For every one of your own cells there's about one of them. They aren't invaders, either: they're residents, and many earn their keep. Meet your microbiome.

cards.fact: About 38 trillion bacteria share your body with about 30 trillion human cells.
cards.context: That's the 2016 estimate from the team behind Level 3's cell count: about 1.3 bacteria per human cell, roughly one to one. For decades, textbooks claimed bacteria vastly outnumbered our own cells, a figure traced to a rough 1970s estimate. Almost all of the bacteria live in the colon.

mascot.line: Science has confirmed it: a trip to the bathroom changes who is in charge.

cards.headline: A little more human after the bathroom
cards.body: Bacteria are small, so all 38 trillion together weigh only about 0.2 kg. And the ratio isn't fixed. Each bowel movement flushes out roughly a quarter to a third of the colon's bacteria, enough to tip the count toward human cells for a while. You are, briefly, a little more human afterwards.

cards.headline: Tenants who pay rent
cards.body: Your gut microbes help break down proteins, fats and carbohydrates in food into nutrients you can absorb, and they make useful compounds, like vitamins, that your own genes can't. Between them, more than 10,000 species carry about 8 million genes, hundreds of times more than your 20,000. You provide the house; they bring the toolbox.

title: How We Learned About the Body
objective: After this level you can describe how dissection and microscopes revealed the body's inner workings.
summary: Galen's anatomy came from animals. In 1543 Vesalius dissected humans himself. Microscopes let Hooke name cells (1665) and Leeuwenhoek see bacteria (1683).

cards.headline: For centuries, doctors learned human anatomy from apes and pigs.
cards.body: Europe's most trusted anatomy books came from Galen, a Greek physician in the Roman Empire, who couldn't dissect human bodies. His books were still the standard in the 1500s. Two new ways of looking changed that: opening up the human body, and magnifying it.

mascot.line: Galen wasn't careless. He just had the wrong patient on the table.

cards.headline: Vesalius looked for himself
cards.body: In 1543, Andreas Vesalius published On the Structure of the Human Body, built on human dissections he did with his own hands. It was more accurate than any description before it, and it caught Galen's slips. Galen had said the human lower jaw is two bones. That's true for a dog. In people, it's one.

events.label: Vesalius's book maps the body from human dissection
Robert Hooke names 'cells' after the boxes he sees in cork

cards.headline: Microbiology began with a set of teeth
cards.body: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek ground his own single lenses, magnifying up to about 300 times. In 1683 he looked at the plaque from his own teeth and saw 'little animalcules' moving about: bacteria, seen for the first time. The microbes you met in Level 8 had been living on people all along. It took a homemade lens to notice them.

title: Checkpoint: The Building Blocks
objective: After this level you can connect cells, DNA, tissues and organs into one picture of how a body is built.
summary: Systems, organs, tissues, cells, DNA: one zoom. About 330 billion cells are replaced daily, and each new cell comes from an old one with a full copy of the DNA.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale: you're being rebuilt while you read this.
cards.body: Every second, millions of your cells are replaced. First, a quick zoom through everything this chapter built. Then, how the building blocks keep renewing themselves.

cards.headline: Zoom from you to a single gene
cards.body: Start with you: 11 organ systems. Zoom into the digestive system and pick one organ, the stomach, built from four tissue types. Zoom into a tissue: similar cells working together, part of about 30 trillion human cells. Open one cell and find the nucleus, holding 46 chromosomes of DNA. Read one gene, and a ribosome builds a protein from its message.

cards.fact: About 330 billion of your cells are replaced every day.
cards.context: That's roughly 1 percent of them, or about 3.8 million every second, according to a 2021 estimate by Ron Sender and Ron Milo. Blood leads the way: about 90 percent of the new cells are blood cells.

mascot.line: Billions of copies a day, and hardly a typo that matters. Best printing press you will ever own.

cards.headline: Every new cell gets the whole book
cards.body: New cells come only from existing cells, one of the rules of cell theory. When a cell divides, each new cell needs an exact copy of the old cell's DNA, and each of DNA's two strands serves as the pattern for a copy. So Level 5's instruction book is being copied all day long, and you never feel a thing.

title: The Skeleton
objective: After this level you can explain what the skeleton does and how many bones an adult has.
summary: An adult has 206 bones, 106 of them in the hands and feet. The axial skeleton guards the brain, heart and lungs; bones also anchor muscles, make blood cells and bank calcium.

cards.headline: Wiggle your fingers and toes. That's more than half your skeleton.
cards.body: Your hands and feet hold more bones than the whole rest of your body. Here's the count for an adult skeleton, how it splits into two teams, and the jobs bones do besides holding you up.

cards.fact: An adult skeleton has 206 bones.
cards.context: Each hand has 27 bones and each foot has 26, so your hands and feet hold 106 of them. That leaves just 100 for everything else: skull, spine, ribs, arms, legs and hips. Your body clearly thinks fingers and toes deserve the fine print.

cards.headline: Two skeletons in one
cards.body: Anatomists split the 206 into two groups. The axial skeleton, 80 bones, is your central column: skull, spine and rib cage. It wraps around your brain, spinal cord, heart and lungs, so its big job is protection. The appendicular skeleton, 126 bones, is your arms and legs plus the shoulder and hip bones that attach them to the column. A bony vault in the middle, limbs bolted on the sides.

mascot.line: A frame, a shield, a bank and a blood factory. Your skeleton has more side jobs than anyone I know.

cards.headline: Much more than a coat hanger
cards.body: Level 1 met the skeletal system as the frame that supports you. That's only job one. Bones give muscles something to pull on, which is how you move. They shield your organs. Red marrow inside some bones makes blood cells, and yellow marrow stores fat. Bone is also a mineral bank for calcium and phosphorus: about 99 percent of your body's calcium is held in your bones and teeth.

title: Inside a Bone
objective: After this level you can explain what bones are made of and how marrow makes blood.
summary: Bone is living tissue: collagen for flexibility, calcium phosphate for hardness. Compact bone outside, spongy bone inside, and red marrow in the spaces makes blood cells.

cards.headline: Your bones are alive, and some of them are making blood right now.
cards.body: The skeleton in a science classroom is dry and dead. Yours is living tissue, full of working cells. Let's cut one open and see what it's made of, and find the factory hidden inside.

cards.headline: Tough fibers, hard crystals
cards.body: Bone is built from two main materials. Collagen, a tough protein, forms fibers that make bone flexible instead of brittle. Crystals of calcium phosphate harden around those fibers and make bone hard and strong. It's a bit like reinforced concrete: a hard material wrapped around a tough framework. Hard enough to hold you up, with just enough give to take a knock.

cards.headline: Solid outside, spongy inside
cards.body: Cut through a bone and you'll find two kinds of bone tissue. Compact bone is the dense, strong outer layer. Inside is spongy bone: a lattice of thin struts called trabeculae, with open spaces between them. The struts form along the lines of stress the bone carries, like scaffolding placed exactly where the load goes.

mascot.line: Every time you sit down, you are sitting on a blood factory. It does not mind at all.

cards.headline: The blood factory
cards.body: Those open spaces in spongy bone hold red marrow, and red marrow makes your blood cells: red blood cells that carry oxygen, white blood cells that fight infection, and platelets that help blood clot. Your hip and thigh bones are among the places it works. Remember Level 10: about 90 percent of the cells your body replaces each day are blood cells. Yellow marrow, the other kind, is mostly fat, an energy store.

title: Joints
objective: After this level you can name the main kinds of joint and explain how they let us move.
summary: A joint is where bones meet. Some never move (skull sutures), some move a little (between vertebrae), and synovial joints move freely, cushioned by cartilage and slick fluid.

cards.headline: Some of your joints never move. That's the point.
cards.body: A joint is anywhere two bones meet. Your knee bends, your shoulder swings in a circle, and the joints in your skull barely move at all. Same word, very different jobs.

cards.headline: Three kinds of joint, sorted by movement

items.label: Immovable
points: Sutures lock the skull's bones together
Their job is protecting the brain

items.label: Slightly movable
points: The discs between the vertebrae of your spine
A little movement, no more

items.label: Freely movable

Built for motion

cards.headline: Why a knee doesn't grind
cards.body: Freely movable joints share one clever design. The bone ends are capped with smooth cartilage and sealed inside a capsule. The capsule's lining makes synovial fluid, a thick, slippery liquid that lubricates the joint and cuts friction between the bones. Every time you bend a knee, cartilage glides over cartilage on a thin slick of fluid.

mascot.line: Door hinges, a swivel and two joysticks. You are carrying a small hardware store around.

title: Broken Bones
objective: After this level you can explain how a broken bone heals.
summary: A fracture is a break in a bone, seen on X-rays because calcium-rich bone shows white. It heals in stages: clot, cartilage callus, spongy bone, then compact bone and remodeling.

cards.headline: A well-healed break can vanish without a trace.
cards.body: When a bone breaks, your body doesn't just glue the pieces together. It rebuilds real bone, and often, once the repair is finished, there's no outside sign the break was ever there. Here's how that happens.

cards.headline: Seeing the break
cards.body: A fracture is simply a break in a bone. Most come from injuries such as falls, car accidents and sports, though overuse and repeated motions can cause them too. To find one, doctors usually take an X-ray. Bones contain calcium, which absorbs X-rays readily, so bone shows up white while muscle and fat appear in shades of gray.

mascot.line: Clot, cartilage, spongy bone, compact bone. Your skeleton repairs itself like a very patient building crew.

cards.headline: Why a broken bone is kept still
cards.body: Healing builds new bone around the pieces wherever they happen to be. A bone that isn't set back in line will heal in its bent position. That's why doctors put the pieces in place and use a cast or splint to keep the bone from moving while it heals. Children run through the same repair stages as adults, only much faster.

cards.headline: Three kinds of muscle are working right now. You're steering one.

mascot.line: Few in number, huge in size. Muscle fibers are the heavyweights of your cell world.

cards.fact: Skeletal muscle cells make up about half of your body's cell mass.

title: How Muscles Pull
objective: After this level you can explain why muscles can only pull and so work in pairs.
summary: Myosin heads pull actin filaments past them, shortening a muscle. A muscle can only pull, so muscles work in pairs: the biceps bends the elbow and the triceps straightens it.

cards.headline: Your muscles can't push. So how do you push a door?
cards.body: Every muscle in your body can only pull. Yet you push doors, shopping carts and elevator buttons all day. The answer is teamwork, and it starts deep inside each muscle fiber.

cards.headline: Tiny hands on a rope
cards.body: Inside a muscle fiber lie two kinds of protein filament: thick ones with myosin heads, and thin ones made of actin. When a signal arrives, the myosin heads grab the actin and pull it, sliding the thin filaments past the thick ones. Each head pulls only a tiny distance, lets go, re-cocks using energy from ATP and grabs again. Picture a crowd of hands hauling in a rope.

cards.headline: Pull only, so muscles come in pairs
cards.body: Sliding filaments can shorten a muscle, but a muscle can only contract, never push. So muscles work in pairs that pull in opposite directions. Your biceps pulls to bend your elbow; your triceps, on the back of your arm, pulls to straighten it. At the knee, the quadriceps straighten and the hamstrings bend. When one partner pulls, the other relaxes.

mascot.line: Push-ups are secretly pull-ups for your triceps. Please do not tell the gym.

cards.headline: Every push is a pull in disguise
cards.body: So how do you push that door? Your triceps pulls to straighten your elbow, and your arm drives forward while the biceps relaxes. No muscle pushed anything. Every push you'll ever make is a pull happening somewhere else.

title: Tendons and Ligaments
objective: After this level you can explain what tendons and ligaments connect.

cards.headline: Your body's thickest tendon is named after a hero's weak spot.
cards.body: In Greek myth, Achilles' heel was the one place he could be hurt. Today his name belongs to the tendon at the back of your heel. So what is a tendon, and what's the thing people always mix it up with?

cards.headline: Built like rope
cards.body: Both are dense connective tissue, the binding-and-supporting tissue type from Level 4. They're packed with collagen, the same tough protein that keeps bone from being brittle, and the fibers are lined up in parallel. Like the strands of a rope, parallel fibers resist stretching in the direction of the pull.

cards.fact: The Achilles tendon is the thickest and most powerful tendon in your body.
cards.context: It connects your calf muscles to your heel. So the legend's famous weak spot is home to your strongest tendon.

mascot.line: Sprain: ligament. Strain: muscle or tendon. The t in strain is for tendon, if that helps.

cards.headline: Two injuries, two tissues
cards.body: A sprain is a stretched or torn ligament. A strain is a stretched or torn muscle or tendon. They sound alike, but they hurt different tissues. And because tendons don't have a rich blood supply, they heal slowly.

title: Getting Stronger
objective: After this level you can explain what happens inside muscles when you exercise.
summary: Muscles grow by thickening fibers with more myofibrils, not by adding cells. Endurance exercise can add mitochondria and capillaries; unused muscle shrinks, but can often recover.

cards.headline: Lifting weights won't give you new muscle cells. It upgrades the old ones.
cards.body: When muscles grow, your body doesn't add new muscle cells. It remodels the ones you already have. What changes depends on how you use them, and on whether you use them at all.

mascot.line: Your muscles do not hire new staff. They promote from within.

cards.headline: Thicker fibers, same number
cards.body: Resistance exercise, such as lifting weights, makes muscle fibers build more myofibrils. Each myofibril is a chain of tiny units holding Level 16's actin and myosin filaments. With more of them packed in, each fiber gets thicker, and so does the muscle. This is called hypertrophy: same cells, more rope-pullers inside each one.

cards.headline: Endurance builds the power supply
cards.body: Long, steady exercise changes muscle in a different way. It can add more mitochondria, the power stations from Level 2 that turn energy from food into a form cells can use. It can also add capillaries, the tiny blood vessels threading through the muscle. More engines, more fuel lines.

cards.headline: Use it or lose it
cards.body: The upgrade runs in reverse, too. When a muscle isn't used, it loses structural proteins and shrinks. That's called atrophy. The good news: atrophy from disuse can often be reversed with exercise. Your muscles keep adjusting to whatever you ask of them.

title: Babies Have More Bones
objective: After this level you can explain how bones grow and fuse from birth to adulthood.
summary: A newborn has roughly 270 to 300 bones. Many start as cartilage, skull gaps close in the first two years, growth plates lengthen bones until early adulthood, and fusion leaves 206.

cards.headline: A newborn has more bones than you do.
cards.body: Estimates put a newborn at roughly 270 to 300 bones. You have 206. Nobody loses bones growing up. They join. Here's how a baby's skeleton becomes yours.

cards.fact: A newborn has roughly 270 to 300 bones; sources vary.
cards.context: Many of them start as cartilage, a tough but flexible tissue. The cartilage doesn't turn into bone; it works as a template that bone gradually replaces. As the skeleton grows, many separate pieces fuse, until the count settles at Level 11's 206.

cards.headline: Soft spots, on purpose
cards.body: At birth the skull's bones aren't yet joined, so the head can change shape on the way through the birth canal. The gaps, called fontanelles, also leave room for the brain to grow. The one at the back usually closes by 1 to 2 months; the one at the front, sometime between 7 and 19 months.

mascot.line: Cartilage on one side, bone on the other. A growth plate is a construction zone that closes when the job is done.

cards.headline: Growth plates: where bones get longer
cards.body: Long bones grow at growth plates, layers of cartilage near each end. On one side of a plate new cartilage forms; on the other it's replaced by bone, so the shaft gets longer. This continues until early adulthood. Then bone replaces the plate entirely, leaving only a thin line, and growth in length is done.

cards.headline: Fusing into one
cards.body: Some bones merge late. Each hip bone starts as three separate bones, the ilium, ischium and pubis, which fuse during the late teens. Your sacrum, at the base of your spine, is five vertebrae fused into a single bone.

title: Checkpoint: Bones and Muscles
objective: After this level you can explain how bones, joints and muscles work together to move you.
summary: Bones are levers, joints are fulcrums and muscles supply the effort. The bent arm trades force for a big, fast movement, and one lift uses nerves, muscle, tendon, joint and ligament together.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 finale: every move you make is a lever.
cards.body: Bones, joints, muscles, tendons: you've met all the parts. Now watch them work as one machine, the same one you use to pull a nail with a hammer.

cards.headline: Levers everywhere
cards.body: Pull a nail with the back of a hammer and you're using a lever: a stiff bar turning on a fixed point, the fulcrum. Your body works the same way. Bones are the stiff levers, joints are the fulcrums, and contracting muscles supply the effort. The load is whatever you're moving, even your own head when you lift it.

mascot.line: Your arm trades strength for speed. Handy for catching things, and for waving hello.

cards.headline: Built for speed, not strength
cards.body: Bend your arm. The elbow is the pivot, and the biceps pulls on the forearm closer to the elbow than the cup in your hand. That costs force: the muscle must pull harder than the load it lifts. In return, a small contraction swings your hand through a large, fast movement. Many of your muscle-and-bone pairs make the same trade.

cards.headline: One sip, the whole chapter
cards.body: Lift that cup. Your nervous system signals the biceps, skeletal muscle you control. Myosin pulls actin, the muscle shortens, and a tendon carries the pull to your forearm bone. The elbow, a hinge joint where ligaments connect the bones, bends. The triceps relaxes, ready to pull back the other way.

title: The Heart
objective: After this level you can explain how the heart's four chambers pump blood.
summary: The heart is a fist-sized pump with four chambers: atria receive blood, ventricles push it out. The right side feeds the lungs, the left the body, and four valves keep it one-way.

cards.headline: Your heart is two pumps sharing one body.
cards.body: It's a muscle about the size of your fist. Look inside, though, and you find four chambers working as two pumps, side by side. Why would one organ need two?

cards.headline: Four rooms: two upstairs, two down
cards.body: Your heart has four chambers. The two upper ones, the atria, are receiving rooms where blood arrives. The two lower ones, the ventricles, are the pumps that push it back out. Picture a house with a front hall above an engine room, on each side. Blood comes in upstairs, drops downstairs and gets shoved out the door.

mascot.line: Right goes to the lungs, left goes everywhere else. Two pumps, one heartbeat, zero arguments about who does more.

cards.headline: Right side to the lungs, left side to everything else
cards.body: The right side handles blood coming home from your body, low on oxygen. It arrives in the right atrium through two big veins, the venae cavae, and the right ventricle pumps it to your lungs. Refilled with oxygen, it returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. Then the left ventricle gives the big push that sends it to your whole body. That's why you need two pumps: one short hop, one very long haul.

cards.fact: Four valves keep your blood on a one-way street.
cards.context: The tricuspid, mitral, pulmonary and aortic valves open to let blood through, then close so it can't flow backward. You can even hear them: the "lub" of a heartbeat is the mitral and tricuspid valves closing, and the "dub" is the aortic and pulmonary valves closing. So the famous sound of your heart isn't the muscle. It's the doors shutting.

title: A Lifetime of Beats
objective: After this level you can explain heart rate and how much blood the heart pumps in a lifetime.
summary: Each beat starts at the SA node in the right atrium. A resting adult heart beats 60 to 100 times a minute, about 100,000 times a day: nearly 2.9 billion beats in a 79-year life.

cards.headline: Press two fingers to your wrist. That tap is your heart at work.
cards.body: Each tap is one heartbeat, and the number in a minute is your heart rate. Now multiply that rhythm by a whole lifetime. How many beats is that, and how much blood gets moved?

cards.headline: Every beat starts with a spark
cards.body: Your heart has its own built-in drummer. Pacemaker cells in the sinoatrial (SA) node, in the right atrium, fire an electrical signal, and the heart muscle contracts in response. At rest, 60 to 100 beats a minute is normal for adults. Young children run faster (80 to 130 at ages 1 to 2), well-trained athletes can idle at 40 to 60, and exercise speeds everyone up. Same drummer, different tempo.

cards.fact: Your heart beats about 100,000 times a day.
cards.context: Each beat pushes only about 70 milliliters of blood out of a ventricle, around 5 liters a minute at rest. But the beats never stop adding up: by bedtime your heart has moved about 7,000 to 8,000 liters of blood. Small sips, enormous total.

mascot.line: Nearly three billion beats and not a single sick day. I would like to meet its manager.

cards.headline: Now multiply by a lifetime
cards.body: Keep that pace for an average life of almost 79 years and your heart beats nearly 2.9 billion times. Over those years it pumps more than 200 million liters of blood. It never takes a weekend off, and it does all of it with a muscle about the size of your fist.

title: Blood Vessels

summary: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins bring it back at low pressure, holding about two-thirds of it. Capillaries, a single cell layer thick, are where delivery happens.

cards.headline: Arteries aren't the "oxygen" ones. They're the "away" ones.
cards.body: You might guess that arteries carry oxygen-rich blood and veins carry the rest. The real rule is simpler, and it's all about which way the blood is heading.

cards.headline: The artery that breaks the color code
cards.body: Here's the proof that direction is the rule. The pulmonary arteries carry blood from your right ventricle to your lungs, and that blood is low in oxygen. They're still arteries, because they lead away from the heart. And the slow, low-pressure veins? At any moment they hold roughly two-thirds of your blood. Arteries are the express lanes; veins are the parking garage.

mascot.line: Single file, no overtaking. The busiest lanes in your body are also the narrowest.

cards.headline: Capillaries: where the delivery happens
cards.body: Arteries and veins are only roads. The drop-off happens in capillaries, vessels so narrow (about 8 to 10 micrometers) that red blood cells squeeze through in single file. Their walls are a single thin layer of cells, so oxygen and nutrients cross out to your tissues and wastes cross in. All the pumping from Level 21 exists to get blood to this doorstep.

summary: Blood is over half plasma, a watery liquid, plus red cells (about 45 percent) that carry oxygen on hemoglobin, and a sliver of white cells and platelets. Adults have about 4 to 6 liters.

cards.headline: Spin a tube of blood and it splits into layers.
cards.body: Put a blood sample in a centrifuge and it separates: plasma on top, a thin pale layer in the middle, red cells at the bottom. Blood is plasma plus red cells, white cells and platelets. So what is each layer doing?

cards.fact: Over half your blood is plasma, and plasma is about 92% water.

cards.headline: Red cells: the oxygen couriers
cards.body: Red blood cells make up about 45 percent of blood's volume, and Level 3 found they are about 84 percent of all your cells. Their job is delivering oxygen from your lungs to your tissues. The carrier is hemoglobin, an iron-containing protein that also gives blood its color. Fresh from the lungs, blood is bright red; after dropping off oxygen, it's a duskier red. Never blue.

cards.headline: The thin pale band
cards.body: That middle layer holds the rest: white blood cells, which fight infection, and platelets, which help blood clot when you cut yourself. Together they're less than 1 percent of a blood sample. The smallest share of blood, doing two of its most urgent jobs. Platelets get their moment in Level 28.

title: Blood Types
objective: After this level you can explain blood types and why they matter for transfusions.
summary: In 1901 Landsteiner found blood groups by watching red cells clump. ABO type depends on A and B antigens on red cells; mismatched antibodies attack donated cells, so transfusions must match.

cards.headline: Giving someone blood used to be a gamble.
cards.body: Blood transfusions stayed risky until an Austrian physician, Karl Landsteiner, discovered the major human blood groups. It turns out your blood carries a label, and the label matters.

cards.headline: The clumping clue
cards.body: In 1901 Landsteiner published what he'd found: mix blood from two people, and sometimes the red cells clump together. The clumping wasn't random. It followed blood groups, the start of the ABO system we still use. The discovery earned him the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Not bad for watching blood misbehave.

cards.headline: Name tags on your red cells
cards.body: Your ABO type depends on two markers, the A and B antigens, sitting on the plasma membrane of your red cells (Level 2's outer wall). Type A has A, type B has B, type AB has both and type O has neither. Your plasma also carries antibodies against any marker you lack: type A blood carries anti-B, type B carries anti-A, type O carries both and type AB carries neither.

mascot.line: O negative: the red cells with no name tags at all, which is exactly what makes them welcome everywhere.

cards.headline: Why a mismatch matters
cards.body: Give someone red cells with a marker their antibodies target, and those antibodies latch on, making the donated cells clump and break apart. There's a second label too: Rh positive or negative, set by the Rh D antigen (about 85 percent of Americans are positive). Type O negative red cells carry no A, B or Rh D, so they can go to anyone in an emergency. Type AB positive people can receive any type.

title: Blood Pressure
objective: After this level you can explain what blood pressure measures and why doctors check it.
summary: Blood pressure is the push of blood on artery walls: systolic over diastolic. The 2025 AHA/ACC guideline sets four categories, and since high pressure is usually silent, only measuring shows it.

cards.headline: 120 over 80. Two numbers, one heartbeat.
cards.body: A blood pressure reading looks like a fraction, but it's really two moments in every heartbeat. What are those numbers measuring, and why do doctors bother checking?

cards.headline: Push, then pause
cards.body: Blood pressure is the force of blood pushing against the walls of your arteries. The top number, systolic, is the pressure as your heart pumps blood out. The bottom number, diastolic, is the pressure between beats, while the heart refills. Both are measured in millimeters of mercury (mm Hg). Think of a garden hose: a surge when the tap opens, a steadier push in between.

title: Harvey and Circulation
objective: After this level you can explain how William Harvey showed that blood circulates.
summary: Galen taught that the liver makes blood the body uses up. In 1628 Harvey showed by arithmetic and a banded arm that blood circulates, and in 1661 Malpighi's microscope found the capillaries.

cards.headline: For about 1,500 years, doctors thought blood was used up like fuel.
cards.body: Galen, the Greek physician in the Roman Empire from Level 9, taught that the liver makes blood, which flows out and is used up by the body. Then, in 1628, an English physician named William Harvey published De Motu Cordis and argued the heart pumps the same blood around in a circuit.

cards.headline: Harvey does the math
cards.body: Harvey estimated how much blood each beat pushes out, keeping his guesses cautious, then multiplied. The heart, he found, pumps far more blood in a day than the whole body weighs. No body could make that much from food and use it all up. There was only one way out of the numbers: the same blood must be going round and round.

mascot.line: No microscope, no scanner, just a band, a thumb and very good arithmetic. Science on a budget.

cards.headline: The banded-arm trick
cards.body: Next, Harvey showed which way it flows. He tied a band around a person's upper arm until the forearm veins swelled and their valves showed. Pressing on a vein, he could push blood toward the heart easily, but not away from it. Remember Level 23's valves in the veins? Harvey read them as one-way signs.

cards.headline: The missing link
cards.body: Harvey had one gap: he couldn't see how blood got from arteries into veins, because capillaries were still unknown. Physicians opposed his theory at first, yet it was well established by the time he died. Then, in 1661, Marcello Malpighi looked at lung tissue under a microscope and described capillaries connecting small arteries with small veins. The circle was closed.

title: How a Cut Heals
objective: After this level you can explain how blood clots and how a cut heals.
summary: A cut stops bleeding in three steps: the vessel narrows, platelets plug the gap and a fibrin mesh sets the clot. Then a scab, a few swollen days and about 3 weeks of rebuilding leave a scar.

cards.headline: You cut your finger. Your blood starts the repair before you find a bandage.
cards.body: Blood usually starts to clot within a few minutes or less. Behind that is a fast three-step emergency response, followed by about 3 weeks of quiet rebuilding.

cards.headline: Squeeze, then plug
cards.body: Stopping the bleeding takes three steps. First, the injured blood vessel narrows, slowing the flow. Second, the platelets from Level 24 arrive. At the damaged wall they turn spiky and sticky, grab onto it and pile onto one another into a plug. Picture a crowd jamming a doorway: not elegant, but nothing gets through.

cards.headline: Step three: the net
cards.body: A plug of platelets alone is flimsy, so the blood clots. Clotting factors, proteins in your blood, work with the platelets to build a tough mesh of fibrin threads that holds everything in place. We know how much this step matters from hemophilia, an inherited disorder in which the blood lacks enough of one clotting factor (factor VIII or IX), so it doesn't clot properly.

mascot.line: A clot, a scab, some swelling and weeks of rebuilding. Your blood runs its own repair crew, no appointment needed.

cards.headline: Then the slow rebuild
cards.body: The clot dries into a scab that shields the tissue underneath from germs. For about 2 to 5 days the area may be a little swollen, red and tender, as blood vessels open to bring in oxygen and nutrients and white blood cells fight germs. Over about 3 weeks, the body repairs broken vessels and fills the gap with new tissue. The scar left behind is smaller than the cut, but less strong and flexible than the skin around it.

title: A Healthy Heart
objective: After this level you can explain what keeps a heart healthy and what harms it.
summary: The heart muscle is fed by the coronary arteries; plaque narrowing them causes coronary heart disease and, if flow is suddenly blocked, a heart attack. The WHO and AHA name what affects heart health.

cards.headline: The heart feeds every part of you. So what feeds the heart?
cards.body: The heart muscle gets its own oxygen-rich blood through its own supply lines, the coronary arteries. When blood flow to part of the heart muscle is suddenly blocked, that's a heart attack. So what do public-health bodies say keeps those lines open?

cards.headline: Clogged supply lines
cards.body: In coronary heart disease, the most common type of heart disease, fatty deposits called plaque build up inside the coronary arteries and narrow them, so less oxygen-rich blood reaches the heart muscle. If blood flow to part of that muscle is suddenly blocked, it's a heart attack, and if flow isn't restored quickly, that part of the muscle begins to die. The pump that feeds everyone can run short of fuel itself.

cards.fact: Cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of death worldwide.
cards.context: The WHO puts them at about a third of all deaths. It also says most cardiovascular disease can be prevented by addressing risk factors, and it names the most important behavioral ones for heart disease and stroke: unhealthy diet, physical inactivity, tobacco use and harmful use of alcohol.

mascot.line: These are what the WHO and AHA say about hearts in general. For your own heart, your doctor is the expert, not this card.

cards.headline: The AHA's eight measures
cards.body: The American Heart Association sums up heart health in a list it calls Life's Essential 8. Four are behaviors: eating better, being more active, quitting tobacco and getting healthy sleep. Four are health factors to manage: weight, cholesterol, blood sugar and blood pressure (the same readings from Level 26). Sleep is the newest entry; the AHA added it in 2022.

title: Checkpoint: Heart and Blood
objective: After this level you can explain how the heart, blood vessels and blood deliver what cells need.
summary: One lap: left ventricle, arteries, capillaries, veins, right heart, lungs and back, passing the heart twice. At rest about 5 liters a minute go through, so your blood laps roughly once a minute.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 finale: ride along with one red blood cell.
cards.body: You've met the pump, the pipes and the passengers. Now follow a single red blood cell on one lap of your body. At rest, your blood passes through your heart about once a minute.

cards.headline: One lap, two circuits
cards.body: Start in the left ventricle. One push sends your red cell out along an artery, branching smaller and smaller until it squeezes single file through a capillary and hands its oxygen to the tissues. Now a duskier red, it drifts home through the veins, with valves keeping it on course, into the right atrium. The right ventricle sends it to the lungs to reload, and it returns to the left side bright red again. One lap, two trips through the heart.

mascot.line: Same blood, lap after lap. Harvey did it with arithmetic; you just did it with one red cell.

cards.fact: At rest, your blood passes through your heart about once a minute.
cards.context: Your heart moves about 5 liters a minute, roughly an adult's whole blood supply. That is the circulation Harvey argued for in 1628: not fresh blood made in the liver and used up, but the same blood going round and round.

title: Why We Breathe
objective: After this level you can explain that cells need oxygen and give off carbon dioxide.
summary: Cells use oxygen to release energy from food, mostly in their mitochondria, and give off carbon dioxide. Each breath out still carries most of the oxygen you breathed in.

cards.headline: Every breath you take is a delivery for your cells.
cards.body: At rest you breathe about 12 to 18 times a minute without giving it a thought. Your lungs don't keep that air. They pass what they need along to your roughly 30 trillion cells. So what do cells want with it, and what do they send back?

mascot.line: Thirty trillion tiny campfires, and not one of them needs a match. Just breathe.

cards.headline: Your cells burn food with oxygen
cards.body: Remember Level 2's mitochondria, the cell's power stations? This is what they need your breath for. In cellular respiration, a cell combines oxygen with molecules from food to release the energy stored inside them, and most of that work happens in the mitochondria. Like any fire, it leaves exhaust: carbon dioxide and water.

cards.headline: Breathing out is taking out the trash
cards.body: Carbon dioxide can't pile up inside you. It passes from your cells into your blood, which has to get rid of it. In your lungs it crosses from the blood into the air, and your next breath out carries it away. So every breath is a two-way trip: oxygen in for your cells, their exhaust out.

cards.fact: You breathe back out most of the oxygen you breathe in.
cards.context: Fresh air is about 21 percent oxygen. The last air leaving your lungs still holds about 16 percent, plus 4 to 5 percent carbon dioxide. Each breath, your body keeps only a slice of the oxygen and swaps in its exhaust. That's why the deliveries never stop: roughly 17,000 to 26,000 breaths a day.

title: The Lungs
objective: After this level you can describe the lungs, the airways and the tiny air sacs.
summary: Air runs down the windpipe and the branching bronchial tree to about 480 million air sacs, where oxygen crosses into the blood. Cilia sweep the airways clean.

cards.headline: Your lungs are an upside-down tree with 480 million leaves.
cards.body: Level 31's oxygen has to get from the air into your blood. The route runs down one trunk, out through thousands of branches, and ends in tiny air sacs with walls so thin that gas slips straight through.

cards.headline: Down the trunk, out along the branches
cards.body: Air comes in through your nose or mouth, passes your voice box and heads down the windpipe. Inside your lungs, the bronchial tubes keep branching (anatomists call it the bronchial tree) into thousands of thinner tubes, the bronchioles. Your right lung has three lobes and your left has two. Every branch ends the same way: in clusters of tiny air sacs called alveoli.

mascot.line: Nobody mentions it at dinner parties, but everybody's airways do it.

cards.headline: Pipes that clean themselves
cards.body: Air brings dust and germs along for the ride. Your airways are lined with cilia, tiny hairlike structures that beat constantly, sweeping a layer of sticky mucus, and everything caught in it, up toward your throat. There it gets swallowed. Yes: you have been quietly swallowing the dust you breathe in for your whole life.

cards.fact: Your lungs hold about 480 million air sacs.
cards.context: That's the average a 2004 study counted in adult lungs, and bigger lungs have more. Each sac is wrapped in tiny blood vessels called capillaries, and the barrier between air and blood is only about 0.5 micrometers thick. Oxygen passes through into the blood; carbon dioxide passes the other way.

title: The Diaphragm
objective: After this level you can explain how the diaphragm moves air in and out.
summary: The dome-shaped diaphragm contracts and moves down, the chest grows, pressure in the lungs falls and air flows in. At rest, breathing out is just the lungs springing back.

cards.headline: You don't suck air in. You make room, and the air comes in by itself.
cards.body: The muscle that does it sits right under your lungs. It is working right now, and you have probably never once seen it. Meet the diaphragm.

cards.headline: A dome that flattens
cards.body: Your diaphragm is a dome-shaped muscle below your lungs, the wall between your chest and your belly, and it's your main breathing muscle. When it contracts, it moves down and makes your chest cavity bigger. Your lungs expand into the new space. It works like pulling back the plunger of a syringe.

cards.headline: Air flows downhill
cards.body: Here's the physics. When your lungs expand, the air pressure inside them drops below the pressure of the air outside. Air always flows from higher pressure to lower pressure, so in it comes. A quiet breath brings in about 500 milliliters, about as much as a small bottle of water.

mascot.line: Breathing out at rest runs on pure bounce. Your lungs are wonderfully lazy.

cards.headline: Breathing out is free
cards.body: At rest, breathing out takes no muscle effort at all. Your diaphragm and rib muscles relax, and your stretchy lungs spring back like an open balloon, pushing the air out. Only when you work hard do the muscles between your ribs, the intercostals, and a few extra muscles join in to force air in and out.

title: Your Voice
objective: After this level you can explain how the vocal cords make sound.
summary: Air from the lungs makes the vocal folds in the larynx vibrate. Their speed sets the pitch; throat, nose, mouth, tongue and lips turn the buzz into words.

cards.headline: Every word you've ever said was made of breath going out.
cards.body: Level 33's diaphragm moves air in and out all day. Your voice borrows the outgoing half. So how does a plain stream of air become a laugh, a whisper or your own name?

cards.headline: Two folds in your voice box
cards.body: Your voice box, the larynx, sits between the base of your tongue and the top of your windpipe. Inside it are the vocal folds (also called vocal cords), two bands of tissue. When you breathe, they stay open. When you speak, they snap together, and air from your lungs blowing past makes them vibrate. That buzz is your voice.

mascot.line: Hum a low note, then a high one. You just retuned your own strings, no guitar required.

cards.headline: A guitar string you tune from the inside
cards.body: How fast your vocal folds vibrate sets your pitch, and when you talk they vibrate more than 100 times a second. Tighten them and the pitch changes, just like tuning a guitar string. Size matters too: vocal folds are shorter and thinner in women and children, which is part of why their voices are higher.

cards.headline: From buzz to words
cards.body: The raw buzz isn't speech yet. The sound travels through your throat, nose and mouth, which shape it as it echoes around inside them. Then your tongue and lips get to work, carving it into words. Your folds make the sound; your mouth makes the meaning.

title: Coughs, Sneezes and Hiccups
objective: After this level you can explain what causes coughs, sneezes and hiccups.
summary: Airway sensors trigger coughs and sneezes to clear out irritants: a cough builds pressure behind the closed glottis, then blasts. A hiccup is a diaphragm spasm cut off by the vocal cords.

cards.headline: Three noisy reflexes, built from parts you already know.
cards.body: Coughs, sneezes and hiccups all happen without asking your permission. Each one takes Level 33's breathing muscles or Level 34's vocal cords and uses them in a sudden, unscheduled way.

cards.headline: The cough: a pressure cannon
cards.body: Sensors in your airways watch for irritants, and when they find one they can set off a cough, a reflex that keeps your throat and airways clear. First you take a deep breath in. Then the glottis, the gap between your vocal cords, stays shut while your breathing-out muscles squeeze, building pressure. Suddenly it opens, and the air blasts out.

cards.headline: The sneeze: aimed through your nose
cards.body: A sneeze is a sudden, forceful, uncontrolled burst of air through your nose and mouth. It's usually set off by something irritating the lining of your nose or throat: pollen, dust, a cold. The same airway sensors that trigger coughs can trigger sneezes. Nobody decides to sneeze. It decides for you.

mascot.line: Two parts, badly timed, one very loud 'hic'. Even your body has clumsy moments.

cards.headline: The hiccup: a breath slammed shut
cards.body: A hiccup is your diaphragm misfiring. It spasms on its own and pulls in a sudden breath, and a split second later your vocal cords snap shut and cut that breath off. The snap is the 'hic'. Hiccups often start for no clear reason, and most bouts fade after a few minutes.

title: Breathing at Altitude
objective: After this level you can explain why breathing is harder high up and how bodies adapt.
summary: Air is about 21 percent oxygen at any height, but pressure falls, so each breath brings less oxygen. Given time, the body acclimatizes with deeper breathing and more red blood cells.

cards.headline: In 1978, two climbers reached the top of Everest on the mountain's own air.
cards.body: Reinhold Messner and Peter Habeler were the first to climb Everest without bottled oxygen. Up there, the air is still about 21 percent oxygen, the same share as at the beach. So why is breathing on a mountaintop so hard?

cards.headline: Same recipe, thinner air
cards.body: The mix never changes; the pressure does. The higher you go, the lower the air pressure, so every breath brings less oxygen into your lungs even though the percentage is the same. At the height of Everest's summit, air pressure is only about 30 percent of its sea-level value. Same gulp, much less oxygen inside it.

mascot.line: Your body can't make the mountain air richer, so it gets better at collecting it.

cards.headline: The body turns up the supply
cards.body: Stay high for a while and your body adapts, a process called acclimatization. You breathe more deeply and faster, your heart beats faster, and over time you make more red blood cells to carry oxygen. It's the body's version of hiring extra delivery drivers when every shipment arrives short.

cards.fact: Altitude sickness usually strikes above about 2,400 meters (8,000 feet).
cards.context: It comes from the lower air pressure and oxygen up high, and it's more likely the faster people climb, before the body has had time to adjust. Symptoms usually fade within 2 to 5 days as acclimatization catches up.

title: Holding Your Breath
objective: After this level you can explain what controls the urge to breathe.
summary: The brainstem runs breathing on autopilot, and its main alarm is rising carbon dioxide. Hyperventilating delays that alarm while oxygen falls, so breath-holding in water can kill.

cards.headline: The urge to breathe isn't mainly your body running out of oxygen.
cards.body: When you hold your breath, the urge to breathe builds fast, and it feels like oxygen running low. Mostly, your body is sensing something else piling up. On land, that's clever physiology. In water, it's a trap.

cards.headline: An autopilot in your brainstem
cards.body: You rarely think about breathing because you don't have to. A respiratory center in the medulla oblongata, part of your brainstem, sets the pace automatically, adjusting to the carbon dioxide, oxygen and acidity in your blood. That's why you have never once forgotten to breathe.

mascot.line: A smoke detector for exhaust. Sensible design, as long as nobody tampers with it.

cards.headline: The alarm is carbon dioxide
cards.body: Surprisingly, the main signal to breathe isn't falling oxygen. It's rising carbon dioxide, Level 31's cell exhaust. As it builds up, it makes your brain more acidic, and that drives you to breathe faster and deeper. Low oxygen only drives breathing once it gets quite low. Your breathing alarm is a smoke detector for exhaust, not a fuel gauge.

cards.headline: Why breath-holding in water is dangerous
cards.body: That design has a deadly gap. Overbreathing before going under (hyperventilating), or long breath-holding, lowers your carbon dioxide first. The alarm is delayed, but oxygen keeps falling, and a swimmer can pass out underwater. The CDC warns that hyperventilating before swimming underwater, or holding your breath underwater for long periods, can cause you to pass out and drown.

cards.fact: In one CDC review of these drownings, all four people who died were advanced swimmers.
cards.context: The report covered 16 incidents in New York State from 1988 to 2011. The four who died were aged 17 to 22, and all had hyperventilated on purpose. Being a strong swimmer didn't protect them.

title: Smoking and the Lungs
objective: After this level you can explain how smoking damages the lungs.
summary: Smoke stalls the airway cilia and adds mucus, causes most US cases of COPD, which damages air sacs and airways, and is linked to about 80 percent of US lung cancer deaths.

cards.headline: Remember Level 32's self-cleaning pipes? Smoke switches the cleaners off.
cards.body: The CDC, the NIH and the WHO agree: smoking harms the lungs, from the airways down to the air sacs. Here's what it does, one part at a time.

cards.headline: The sweepers stall
cards.body: Cigarette smoke paralyzes and damages the cilia that sweep your airways clean, and it makes the airways produce more mucus. So the escalator from Level 32 slows down just as more mucus arrives. The clearing of mucus, the airway's everyday cleanup, falls behind.

cards.headline: Damage deep in the lungs
cards.body: In the US, smoking is the main cause of COPD, a disease of damage to the airways or other parts of the lung. In emphysema, the walls between many air sacs are damaged: the same thin walls where oxygen crosses into your blood. In chronic bronchitis, the airway lining stays irritated and inflamed. COPD has no cure.

cards.fact: About 80 percent of US lung cancer deaths are linked to cigarette smoking.
cards.context: The CDC says people who smoke are 15 to 30 times more likely to get or die from lung cancer. Smoke from other people's cigarettes causes it too, and the WHO says there is no safe level of tobacco exposure. The CDC also notes that a person's lung cancer risk goes down after they quit.

title: Asthma
objective: After this level you can explain what happens in an asthma attack and how inhalers help.
summary: In an asthma attack the airways swell, narrow, make extra mucus and may tighten. Asthma has no cure but is managed with medical care; inhalers deliver medicine straight to the lungs.

cards.headline: Imagine trying to breathe in through a straw.
cards.body: That's how some people describe an asthma attack. Asthma is the most common chronic disease among children. So what is actually happening inside the airways?

cards.headline: Airways that squeeze shut
cards.body: Asthma is a long-term condition of the airways in the lungs. During an attack, the airways become inflamed, swell and narrow, and can make extra mucus. The muscles wrapped around them may tighten too. Air has to squeeze through a narrower tube, which makes breathing harder, especially breathing out. It can bring coughing, wheezing and a tight chest.

cards.headline: Something sets it off
cards.body: Attacks often have a trigger. Pollen, dust, smoke, fumes, cold air, viral infections and even exercise can set off or worsen asthma symptoms. Smoke, the villain of Level 38, is on the list again.

mascot.line: Straight to the airways, no detour. That's what an inhaler is for.

cards.headline: Managed with medical care
cards.body: There's no cure for asthma, but it can be managed. People with asthma work with a healthcare provider on a written asthma action plan that sets out which medicines to take and when. Inhalers deliver asthma medicine directly to the lungs. Quick-relief medicines open narrowed airways during an attack; daily controller medicines reduce inflammation to help prevent attacks.

title: Checkpoint: Breathing
objective: After this level you can trace a breath of air from your nose to your cells and back out again.
summary: The nose warms, moistens and filters air. Then down the bronchial tree to the air sacs, into the blood, to the cells' mitochondria, and back out as carbon dioxide.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 finale: follow one breath all the way in and back out.
cards.body: You've met every part of the trip. Now ride along with a single breath, starting at a doorway you've barely thought about: your nose.

cards.headline: Your nose is an air conditioner
cards.body: Before air reaches your lungs, your nose (and your mouth, when you breathe through it) warms and moistens it, because cold, dry air can irritate the lungs. Hairs just inside your nostrils block bigger bits of dirt, and the airways beyond keep working to remove debris and germs. By the time a breath reaches your chest, it has been warmed, dampened and filtered.

mascot.line: One breath, two deliveries, zero paperwork. Your lungs run a very tidy courier service.

cards.headline: The round trip
cards.body: Down the windpipe, out along the bronchial tree, through thousands of bronchioles to about 480 million air sacs. Oxygen crosses their thin walls into the blood and rides to your cells, where mitochondria use it to release energy from food. The exhaust, carbon dioxide, rides the blood back, crosses into the air sacs, and leaves as your diaphragm relaxes and your lungs spring back.

title: A Journey Through Digestion
objective: After this level you can trace food from the mouth through the intestines.
summary: Food travels one tube from mouth to anus, pushed by waves of muscle called peristalsis, not by gravity. Helper organs add juices, the small intestine absorbs, the large intestine takes back water.

cards.headline: In 1962, John Glenn ate applesauce in orbit.
cards.body: On February 20, 1962, aboard Friendship 7, he squeezed it from a tube while floating weightless. Down was no longer a direction, yet the applesauce went where it should. So what moves food through you, if not gravity? Follow one bite all the way through.

cards.headline: One tube, open at both ends
cards.body: Your digestive tract is one long tube: mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, anus. Because it opens to the outside at both ends, food inside it is technically still outside your body until it's absorbed. That sandwich isn't part of you yet. It's just passing through the tunnel.

mascot.line: Try it with a sip of water while lying down. Your esophagus does not care which way is up.

cards.headline: Squeezed, not dropped
cards.body: Food doesn't fall down the tube. It's pushed. Waves of muscle contraction called peristalsis squeeze it along, a bit like squeezing toothpaste from the bottom of the tube. Gravity isn't needed, so swallowed food can travel your esophagus even when you're upside down. That's why Glenn's applesauce went the right way in orbit.

cards.headline: Helpers along the route
cards.body: Some digestive organs sit beside the tube instead of in it. The liver, pancreas and gallbladder add digestive juices. The small intestine then absorbs most of the nutrients from your food. What's left moves into the large intestine, which includes the colon: water is absorbed there, and the leftovers become stool. The colon is also where almost all of Level 8's bacteria live. Last stop, busiest neighborhood.

title: The Stomach
objective: After this level you can explain how the stomach breaks food down with acid.
summary: Beaumont watched a living stomach through a healed gunshot wound. Acid and pepsin break food down, muscles churn it into chyme, and mucus and fast renewal protect the wall.

cards.headline: A gunshot wound gave one doctor a window into a stomach.
cards.body: For centuries physicians argued about what the stomach does. Some thought it cooked food with inner heat; others blamed fermentation or rotting. Then, in 1822, an accident on the Michigan frontier let a doctor look inside a living one.

cards.headline: The window into a stomach
cards.body: Alexis St. Martin was a 19-year-old fur trapper when he was shot at close range. Army surgeon William Beaumont treated him, and the wound healed with a permanent opening into his stomach. Beaumont lowered foods in on a silk string to time their digestion and drew out gastric juice. His 1833 book reported that the juice held hydrochloric acid and dissolved food. It came at a cost: St. Martin reported pain during some experiments, and once left for Canada without Beaumont's consent.

cards.headline: Acid and a protein cutter
cards.body: The juice Beaumont collected comes from glands in your stomach lining. It carries hydrochloric acid, strong enough to kill many swallowed bacteria. The acid also switches on pepsin, an enzyme that breaks down proteins. Meanwhile Level 4's three layers of smooth muscle churn everything together until your meal becomes a thick liquid called chyme, ready for the small intestine.

mascot.line: A bag full of acid that keeps itself intact by never standing still. Respect.

cards.headline: Why it doesn't digest itself
cards.body: So why doesn't all that acid and pepsin digest the stomach too? A thick coat of mucus, rich in bicarbonate that neutralizes acid, lines the wall. And the surface lining is replaced every few days. The stomach doesn't avoid the damage. It simply outpaces it.

title: The Intestines
objective: After this level you can explain how the intestines absorb nutrients.
summary: Villi and microvilli let the small intestine absorb almost all nutrients. In 2014 the gut lining measured 30 to 40 square meters, not a tennis court. The large intestine takes back water.

cards.headline: Your gut's lining was said to be as big as a tennis court.
cards.body: Textbooks repeated it for decades: 180 to 300 square meters inside you. Then, in 2014, two scientists measured it properly. The real answer is smaller, but still big enough to explain how you absorb a meal.

cards.headline: Where food becomes you
cards.body: Your small intestine is where most digestion happens and almost all nutrients are absorbed. Its lining isn't smooth. It's covered in tiny finger-like projections called villi, and the cells on the villi carry even tinier ones called microvilli. Think of a bath towel next to a sheet of plastic: all those loops give far more surface to soak things up.

cards.fact: Your gut's inner surface is about 30 to 40 square meters: half a badminton court.
cards.context: Herbert Helander and Lars Fändriks found that in 2014 using microscope measurements. Older textbooks said 180 to 300 square meters, a tennis court or more. Most of the real area is in the small intestine; the large intestine adds only about 2 square meters. Smaller than the legend, still roomy.

cards.headline: Into the blood, then the colon
cards.body: Once absorbed, simple sugars, amino acids and some vitamins and salts travel in your blood to the liver first, while fatty acids take a side route through the lymphatic system. Whatever isn't absorbed moves on to the large intestine. There water is absorbed, and bacteria break down remaining nutrients and make vitamin K. Level 8's microbes get the leftovers and pay you back in vitamins.

title: The Liver
objective: After this level you can name the many jobs the liver does.
summary: The liver, the largest gland, meets absorbed nutrients first. It makes bile, stores glycogen and vitamins, clears wastes and old red blood cells, and can grow back after up to two-thirds is removed.

cards.headline: In Greek myth, an eagle ate Prometheus's liver. It kept growing back.
cards.body: That was Zeus's punishment: the liver regrew, so the torment never ended. Myth, of course. But real livers have a surprising talent for regrowing too. First, though: what does this organ actually do all day?

cards.headline: First stop after the gut
cards.body: Your liver is the largest gland in your body, about 1.2 to 1.6 kg in an adult. Remember Level 44? Blood from your intestines goes to the liver first, carrying the sugars and amino acids you just absorbed. The liver stores and processes those nutrients and sends them on to the rest of your body when they're needed. Every meal clears customs here.

title: The Kidneys
objective: After this level you can explain how the kidneys filter the blood.
summary: Two fist-sized kidneys hold about a million nephrons each. A glomerulus filters the blood and a tubule takes back what's needed: of 150 to 180 liters filtered a day, about 99 percent returns.

cards.headline: Your kidneys filter 150 to 180 liters a day, then hand back 99 percent.
cards.body: That sounds wasteful, like emptying the whole kitchen cupboard to find one spoon. It's actually a clever way to clean blood. Here's how two fist-sized organs pull it off.

cards.headline: Two fists, a million filters each
cards.body: Your kidneys are two bean-shaped organs, each about the size of a fist, tucked just below your rib cage on either side of your spine. Each holds about a million tiny filtering units called nephrons. They're the working heart of Level 1's urinary system, the team that removes waste from the blood and balances water.

cards.headline: Filter first, then take back
cards.body: In each nephron, blood first passes a filter called the glomerulus. Water, wastes and other small molecules get through; blood cells and proteins are held back. Then a tubule returns the substances your body still needs to the blood. What's left is waste in a little water: urine. Throw out almost everything, then keep the good stuff.

mascot.line: Recycling rate: about 99 percent. Your kidneys would win any sustainability award.

cards.fact: About 99 percent of what your kidneys filter goes back into your blood.
cards.context: Of the 150 to 180 liters filtered each day, only about 1 to 2 liters leave as urine. It's Level 7's water doing one of its day jobs: a small share carries wastes out of your body, and the rest goes straight back into circulation.

title: Calories
objective: After this level you can explain what a calorie measures.
summary: A calorie is a unit of energy; the food Calorie is a kilocalorie. Atwater's room-sized calorimeter showed energy is conserved in people. How much energy a body uses varies from person to person.

cards.headline: A calorie is a unit, like a meter.
cards.body: It measures energy, the way a meter measures length. It isn't a score or a verdict on a food. So what exactly does it measure, and how did anyone measure the energy a person uses?

mascot.line: Nobody calls a meter good or bad. A calorie is the same kind of thing: a unit.

cards.headline: Warming a gram of water
cards.body: One calorie is the heat it takes to warm 1 gram of water by 1 °C. That's tiny, so food labels use a bigger unit: the Calorie with a capital C, which is a kilocalorie, 1,000 small calories. When food is broken down, its energy is released, and your cells spend it on everything they do, from building proteins on up.

cards.headline: A room built to measure people
cards.body: In 1896 at Wesleyan University, Wilbur Atwater's team began about 500 experiments in a respiration calorimeter: a small sealed room where volunteers stayed, sometimes for days, while the heat and carbon dioxide they gave off were measured. It showed that the law of conservation of energy holds for people too, and let the team work out the energy in foods: about 4 Calories per gram for protein or carbohydrate, about 9 for fat.

cards.headline: Every body runs its own budget
cards.body: How much energy a body uses isn't one number. It varies with age, sex, body size, physical activity and each person's metabolic rate, so no single figure fits everyone. Much of it goes on work you never notice. Your brain is about 2 percent of an adult's body weight but uses about 20 percent of the body's calories, at a fairly steady rate whether you're solving puzzles or daydreaming.
