title: Vitamins and Scurvy
objective: After this level you can explain why vitamins matter, using scurvy as the example.
summary: Without vitamin C the body can't make collagen properly, and scurvy follows. James Lind saw citrus work in 1747, but blamed scurvy on digestion and damp air; the Navy acted in 1795.

cards.headline: In 1747, a ship's surgeon saw citrus beat scurvy. The Navy acted 48 years later.
cards.body: It's often told as a quick triumph: a doctor tries lemons, sailors are saved. The real story is slower, and more interesting. First, what was scurvy doing to those sailors?

cards.headline: The missing ingredient
cards.body: Scurvy is what happens without enough vitamin C. Your body needs it to make collagen, the protein that holds skin, blood vessels, bones and cartilage together. Without it, connective tissue weakens: tiredness, aching joints, swollen and bleeding gums, loose teeth, wounds that won't heal. Signs can appear within about a month, and untreated scurvy can kill. Many animals make their own vitamin C. Humans can't; we lack a working enzyme to do it.

mascot.line: A good experiment can still be misread by the person who ran it. Science keeps checking.

cards.headline: Why the lesson took 48 years

He blamed scurvy mainly on damp air and a coarse diet the body failed to digest, not on a missing nutrient. He later recommended rob, a juice concentrate made by heating, and heat destroys vitamin C. The Admiralty adopted lemon juice in 1795, persuaded by Gilbert Blane. The evidence came early; the explanation came much later.

title: Milestone: Fuel and Oxygen

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Follow one bite all the way to a cell.
cards.body: You've taken food down the tube, through the stomach and intestines, and past the liver. One question is left: where does the energy in your lunch actually get used? The answer is inside your cells.

cards.headline: From lunch to a power station
cards.body: Digestion breaks the starch in your lunch into simple sugars, and your body turns them into glucose, your cells' main fuel. The small intestine absorbs it, and your blood takes it to the liver first, then on to cells all over your body. Inside each cell, Level 2's mitochondria convert the energy from food into a form the cell can use. Fuel you don't need right away can be stored in the liver, muscles and body fat.

mascot.line: Your sandwich and your last breath have a meeting scheduled. Location: a mitochondrion near you.

cards.headline: Fuel meets oxygen
cards.body: Mitochondria can't release that energy from fuel alone. In cellular respiration, cells combine oxygen with food molecules to free their chemical energy. That oxygen comes from your lungs into your blood, and your cardiovascular system carries it, along with the nutrients, to the tissues: Level 1's teamwork again. Breakfast and breath end up in the same tiny place.

title: The Nervous System
objective: After this level you can explain how the brain, the spinal cord and the nerves connect.
summary: The brain and spinal cord are the central nervous system; nerves everywhere else are the peripheral one. Messages run both ways, and much of the work runs without you.

cards.headline: Wiggle your toes. A message just made a round trip.
cards.body: Back in Level 1, the nervous system's job was to sense and respond. To move your toes, orders ran from your brain, down your spinal cord and out along nerves to your foot muscles. This level maps that wiring.

cards.headline: Head office and the roads out
cards.body: Anatomists split the nervous system in two. The central nervous system is your brain and spinal cord, packed safely inside your skull and your backbone. The peripheral nervous system is everything else: the nerves that branch out to every corner of you. Think of a head office with a road to every branch. The decisions happen at head office; the roads are how news and orders get there and back.

cards.fact: Nerves are two-way streets.
cards.context: Sensory neurons carry information in, from your sense organs toward your brain. Motor neurons carry messages out, from your brain to your muscles, down the spinal cord and along the nerves. Stub your toe and the news travels up; decide to hop around the kitchen and the orders travel down.

mascot.line: Imagine having to remember to sweat. Nobody would get anything else done.

cards.headline: You choose to wave. You never choose to sweat.
cards.body: Some responses are voluntary, like contracting the skeletal muscles that wave your hand. The somatic nervous system runs those. Others are involuntary: heart muscle, the smooth muscle in your organs, and glands such as your sweat glands. The autonomic nervous system handles them, no permission needed.

title: Neurons
objective: After this level you can explain how a neuron sends a signal.
summary: Your brain has about 86 billion neurons. Each takes messages in through dendrites and sends them down an axon: electrical along the wire, chemical across the gap.

cards.headline: For decades the textbooks said 100 billion. Nobody had counted.
cards.body: It was a nice round number of neurons, with no published count behind it. In 2009, a team finally did the counting, and the answer came out smaller. Then comes the better question: how does each one of those cells pass a message on?

mascot.line: Brain soup, for science. Not a recipe I'll be sharing.

cards.fact: Your brain has about 86 billion neurons.
cards.context: Frederico Azevedo and colleagues dissolved brain tissue into an even soup of loose cell nuclei, stained and counted the nuclei in samples, then scaled up. Across four men's brains, the average was about 86 billion neurons, with about 85 billion other cells alongside them. Not quite 100 billion, but nobody's complaining.

cards.headline: Dendrites listen, the axon talks
cards.body: A neuron has three parts. Dendrites branch out like a tree and receive messages. The cell body holds the nucleus, Level 2's command center. The axon is a long tail that sends the message on to another neuron, a muscle or another cell. Some axons reach less than a hair's width; others run from your brain all the way down your spinal cord. Information flows one way: dendrites, cell body, axon.

cards.headline: Electric along the wire, chemical across the gap
cards.body: Neurons use electrical and chemical signals. A signal races along the axon electrically, helped by myelin, a fatty wrapping that insulates it so signals travel faster and farther. At the axon's end, tiny sacs release chemicals called neurotransmitters into a tiny gap, the synapse. They cross it and attach to the next cell. So every neuron is part wire, part postbox.

title: Reflexes
objective: After this level you can explain why some reflexes happen before you can think.
summary: Reflexes take a shortcut through the spinal cord, so your hand leaves a hot stove before you register the pain. The knee jerk is a stretch reflex.

cards.headline: Touch a hot stove and your hand moves before you feel it.
cards.body: You pull away, typically before you have even registered the pain. So who made the decision, if it wasn't the thinking you?

cards.headline: A shortcut through the spine
cards.body: Sensors in your skin detect the heat. A signal races along a sensory fiber to your spinal cord, where it connects to a motor neuron. That neuron fires, your biceps contracts, and your hand is off the stove. Simple reflexes like this skip the brain's higher centers, the ones you use for deliberate moves. The spinal cord makes the call, and the brain gets the memo afterwards.

cards.fact: The doctor's rubber hammer tests a stretch reflex.
cards.context: Tap the tendon below your kneecap and your leg kicks: that's the knee jerk. When a muscle is stretched, a sensor inside it makes the same muscle contract, helping keep muscles at a steady length. Here the sensory neuron connects straight to the motor neuron, which makes it very fast. It's why your head jerks back up when you nod off sitting up.

mascot.line: Your spinal cord: not much of a thinker, but a brilliant bodyguard.

cards.headline: Built for speed, down to the details
cards.body: The withdrawal reflex even clears its own path. While the biceps pulls your arm back, the spinal cord stops the opposing triceps from contracting, so the two muscles don't fight and the withdrawal is faster. Fewer steps, no committee meeting upstairs: that is how a reflex beats a thought.

cards.body: The brain works like a team of experts: every part pitches in, but each has its own responsibilities. Meet the three main players and the four neighborhoods of the biggest one. Then find out which small part holds about 80 percent of the staff.

cards.headline: Four lobes, four neighborhoods
cards.body: The cerebrum's surface divides into lobes. The frontal lobes, behind your forehead, plan and drive voluntary movement. The parietal lobes take in touch and temperature. The temporal lobes handle hearing and help form memories. The occipital lobes, at the back, process images from the eyes; damage there can cause blindness. So you're reading this with the back of your head.

title: Left Brain, Right Brain?
objective: After this level you can explain what the two halves of the brain do and why "left-brained" is a myth.
summary: Two hemispheres, linked by the corpus callosum, each run the opposite side of the body, and language leans left. But no one is left-brained or right-brained.

cards.headline: Logical or creative? The quiz says you're one side. Scans disagree.
cards.body: A popular idea says logical, detail-minded people are left-brained and creative, subjective people are right-brained. There is real science about the brain's two halves. The personality labels are where it falls apart.

cards.headline: Two halves, one cable, crossed wires
cards.body: A deep groove splits your cerebrum into two halves, the hemispheres. They talk through the corpus callosum, a thick bundle of nerve fibers. And the wiring crosses over: your right hemisphere mainly controls the left side of your body, and the left hemisphere the right. That's why a stroke in the right hemisphere can paralyze the left arm and leg. Wave your right hand: that was the left side of your brain.

cards.headline: Some jobs really do lean to one side
cards.body: The halves aren't identical twins. For most people, forming words and speech rely mainly on the left hemisphere, while the right takes the lead in spatial tasks and attention. So the brain does split some work. The question is whether whole people split too.

mascot.line: Good news for quiz-takers: you don't have to pick a side.

cards.fact: Nobody is left-brained or right-brained.
cards.context: In 2013, Jared Nielsen, Jeff Anderson and colleagues at the University of Utah analyzed resting brain scans of 1,011 people aged 7 to 29, split into about 7,000 regions. Particular connections leaned left or right, like the language areas, but no one had a stronger left or right network overall. Lopsided jobs, yes. Lopsided people, no.

title: Memory
objective: After this level you can explain how memories are made and why we forget.
summary: Henry Molaison lost his hippocampus and could not make new long-term memories, yet learned skills. Forgetting is fastest right after learning; spacing study helps.

cards.headline: In 1953, one surgery stopped a man making new memories.
cards.body: Henry Molaison was 27 when surgeons operated to control his severe seizures. Afterward, he could meet you and chat, and minutes after you left the room, have no memory of the meeting. His loss showed science where new memories are made.

cards.headline: The library was fine. The librarian was gone.
cards.body: Surgeons had removed tissue from each side of his brain, including much of the hippocampus. That small structure deep in the brain acts as a memory indexer: it sends new memories to the right part of the cerebrum for long-term storage and fetches them back. Molaison kept memories from before surgery, like scenes from his childhood. He just couldn't file new ones.

cards.fact: He got better at a skill he never remembered practicing.
cards.context: Molaison practiced tracing patterns while watching his hand in a mirror. Over time he improved, yet each time he could not recall ever doing the task. Skills like this rely on different memory systems from the hippocampus. Memory, it turns out, isn't one thing.

mascot.line: If this level fades a bit by tomorrow, that's Ebbinghaus's curve. Come back and nudge it.

cards.headline: Why you forget, and how to fight back
cards.body: In 1885, Hermann Ebbinghaus published results from testing his own memory with nonsense syllables. His forgetting curve showed that forgetting is fastest soon after learning, then slows. Later research found a fix: spacing study out over time beats cramming it into one session. It's one of the most replicated findings in psychology. Little and often wins.

title: Sleep
objective: After this level you can explain what happens in the body and brain during sleep.
summary: Sleep cycles through three non-REM stages and REM several times a night. Why we sleep is still debated, from memory to cleaning the brain.

cards.headline: You spend about a third of your life asleep. Your brain stays busy.
cards.body: Your brain and body stay remarkably active while you sleep. The night runs on a schedule of stages, and scientists are still arguing about what it's all for.

events.label: A few minutes of changeover: heartbeat and breathing slow, muscles twitch

cards.headline: Then round again
cards.body: You don't pass through the stages once. You cycle through non-REM and REM sleep several times a night. Deep stage 3 comes in longer stretches in the first half of the night, while REM periods grow longer later on. So the early night is deep-sleep country, and the small hours belong more and more to REM.

cards.headline: Why sleep? The honest answer
cards.body: Everyone needs sleep, but its biological purpose remains a mystery. One strong clue: storing memories, the hippocampus job from Level 56, most likely needs both non-REM and REM sleep. Your brain spends the night filing, not just resting.

mascot.line: Two good labs, opposite answers. Stay tuned; that is how science gets settled.

cards.fact: Does sleep clean the brain? Scientists are still arguing.
cards.context: In 2013, a study in mice led by Maiken Nedergaard suggested the space between brain cells grows during sleep, letting fluid flush out toxins built up while awake. In 2024, a mouse study by Nicholas Franks, William Wisden and colleagues found clearance was reduced during sleep instead. The debate continues, which is how science is supposed to work.

title: Dreams

cards.headline: In 1951, a machine said a sleeping boy was wide awake.

cards.fact: Wake someone when their eyes dart, and they'll tell you a dream.

Most are forgotten by breakfast.

title: Hormones and Feelings
objective: After this level you can explain how hormones like adrenaline shape the way we feel.
summary: Nerves send fast, local messages; hormones travel in the blood. In a scare, nerves trigger the adrenal glands, and adrenaline readies the body to fight or flee.

cards.headline: Before a big test, your heart pounds and your mouth goes dry.
cards.body: You never asked for either. Deep in your brain, the hypothalamus gets the adrenaline flowing during a test or a job interview, and adrenaline brings a racing heart and a dry mouth. Here's how a feeling turns into a body-wide event.

cards.headline: Nerves text. Hormones broadcast.
cards.body: Level 1 gave the endocrine system one job: sending hormones. Here's how they differ from nerves. A nerve's chemical message acts locally, and the target cell responds within milliseconds. Hormones are released by glands into the blood and travel all over the body to their targets, so they usually act more slowly; some take up to 48 hours. A nerve is a text to one person. A hormone is an announcement over the loudspeaker.

cards.headline: The fast lane to adrenaline
cards.body: So how does a scare hit you in seconds? The two systems team up. In danger or stress, a nerve pathway from the hypothalamus triggers your adrenal glands, which release epinephrine, better known as adrenaline, into the blood within seconds. The quick nervous system lights the fuse; the blood carries the hormone everywhere.

cards.fact: Adrenaline preps you to fight or run.
cards.context: Walter Cannon coined 'fight or flight' in the early 1900s. Adrenaline raises your heart rate and blood pressure, widens your airways and pupils, and releases sugar into your blood for fuel. It diverts blood from your gut and skin to your muscles and brain. The dry mouth and vanished appetite? Digestion has been put on hold.

title: More Than Five Senses
objective: After this level you can explain why we have more than the classic five senses.
summary: Aristotle listed five senses, but balance, body position, temperature, pain and hunger are senses too. The count depends on how you define one: from six or seven to 22 to 33.

cards.headline: Close your eyes and touch your nose. Which of the five senses did that?
cards.body: Not sight, and not hearing, smell or taste. Not really touch either, since your hand found your nose before it felt it. You just used a sense that isn't on the famous list. So where did the list come from, and how many senses do you actually have?

cards.headline: Aristotle's famous five
cards.body: The classic list comes from Aristotle, the ancient Greek philosopher. In his book On the Soul (De Anima) he named sight, hearing, touch, taste and smell, and then argued there could be no sixth. The list stuck so well that it still feels like a law of nature. It's really a philosopher's tally, and tallies can be redone.

mascot.line: Five senses on the brochure, a whole staff working backstage.

cards.headline: The senses nobody listed
cards.body: Receptors in your muscles, tendons and joints keep a running report on where your limbs are and how they move: that's how you found your nose. Organs in your inner ear give you balance. You also sense temperature and pain, and receptors in your gut help create hunger and thirst. None of them made Aristotle's list. All of them are on duty right now.

cards.fact: So how many senses do you have? It depends on how you count.
cards.context: In 2024, three neurologists proposed adding balance and body position, for six or seven. Philosopher Barry Smith reports that colleagues of neuroscientist Charles Spence put the number anywhere between 22 and 33. The argument isn't about hidden organs; it's over what counts as one separate sense. Is sensing heat one sense, or part of touch? The safe answer is simply: more than five.

title: How Eyes See
objective: After this level you can explain how the eye focuses light and the brain builds a picture.
summary: The cornea and lens focus light on the retina, whose photoreceptors signal the brain via the optic nerve. The brain turns the upside-down image upright and fills in the blind spot.

cards.headline: Your eye takes every picture upside down. You've never noticed.
cards.body: The image that lands at the back of your eye is inverted, yet the world looks the right way up. Follow a beam of light through your eye to find out who does the fixing.

cards.headline: Bend, then focus
cards.body: Light first passes through the cornea, the clear dome at the front of your eye, which bends it. Some of that light gets in through the pupil, an opening whose size is set by the colored iris around it. Next comes the lens, which works with the cornea to focus the light onto the retina, a light-sensitive layer of tissue at the back. Two lenses in a row, and no focus ring to twist.

mascot.line: A camera that shoots upside down, with a darkroom that fixes every frame for free.

cards.headline: The brain develops the picture
cards.body: In the retina, special cells called photoreceptors turn light into electrical signals. The optic nerve carries those signals to your brain, which turns them into the images you see. Because the cornea and lens together act like one convex lens, the image on the retina is upside down, and your brain corrects for it. Your eye collects the light. Your brain does the seeing.

cards.fact: Each of your eyes has a blind spot, and you're not seeing it right now.
cards.context: It sits where the optic nerve leaves the retina, a patch with no rods or cones, so nothing landing there is detected. You don't notice the hole because your two eyes' views overlap, and even with one eye shut your brain fills in or ignores the gap. Your brain isn't just receiving the picture. It's quietly editing it.

title: Seeing Color
objective: After this level you can explain how we see color and what color blindness is.
summary: Three cone types, blended by the brain, give color. Red-green color blindness affects about 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women (Northern European ancestry): its genes are on the X.

cards.headline: In 1794, a chemist reported that his own eyes saw color strangely.
cards.body: John Dalton told a Manchester society that he and his brother saw colors differently from other people. It was the first published account of color blindness. To see what went different for Dalton, first see how color works for you.

mascot.line: Three dials, one mixing desk, and every sunset you have ever seen.

cards.headline: Three kinds of cone
cards.body: Your retina has two kinds of light-sensing cell. Rods handle dim light. Cones work in bright light and give you color. There are three types of cone, each with a pigment most sensitive to a particular range of wavelengths, and your brain combines the input from all three. Every color you have ever seen is your brain's blend of three readings.

cards.headline: Why it's mostly men
cards.body: The most common color vision deficiency makes red and green hard to tell apart. Among people of Northern European ancestry it affects about 1 in 12 men but only 1 in 200 women. The reason is in Level 5's chromosomes: the genes behind it sit on the X chromosome. Men have one X, so one copy is enough. Women have two, and need the gene on both.

cards.fact: Dalton blamed a blue tint inside his eyes. His own eye proved him wrong.
cards.context: He guessed the jelly-like fluid in his eyes was tinted blue, and asked for them to be examined after his death. In 1844 they were: the fluid was colorless. In 1995, DNA from his preserved eye showed he lacked the gene for the green-sensitive cone pigment. He was right that his eyes differed, just wrong about why.

title: Glasses and Contacts
objective: After this level you can explain how lenses correct short and long sight.
summary: Nearsighted eyes focus light in front of the retina, farsighted eyes behind it. Concave lenses push the focus back; convex lenses pull it forward. Contacts work the same way.

cards.headline: Raphael painted a pope holding a lens that curves inward.
cards.body: In the portrait, from the late 1510s, Pope Leo X holds a concave lens: he was nearsighted. It's an early picture of a lens for blurry distance vision, and today's glasses still work on the same idea. To see why, start with what goes wrong inside the eye.

cards.headline: Focus in the wrong place
cards.body: Remember Level 62: your cornea and lens should focus light right on the retina. When the eye's shape is a little off, the focus misses. In nearsightedness, or short sight, the eyeball is often too long, so light focuses in front of the retina and far-away things blur. In farsightedness, or long sight, it's often too short, so light focuses behind the retina and nearby things blur. Same camera, focus set slightly wrong.

mascot.line: Glasses don't fix the eye. They just meet it halfway, one bend at a time.

cards.headline: Bend it back
cards.body: A lens in front of your eye moves the focus. A concave lens, thinner in the middle, spreads light rays apart, pushing the focus back onto the retina: the fix for nearsightedness. A convex lens, thicker in the middle, brings rays together and pulls the focus forward, which helps farsighted eyes. A contact lens does the same job as a thin lens worn right on the surface of your eye.

cards.fact: The first glasses helped people see up close.
cards.context: The earliest eyeglasses, which in Europe first appeared in Italy, had convex lenses to help farsighted people. Lenses for the opposite problem came later, which is why the pope's concave lens is worth a close look. Eyes that blurred up close got help first.

title: How Ears Hear
objective: After this level you can explain how the ear turns sound waves into signals.
summary: The eardrum vibrates, three tiny bones amplify, and the fluid-filled cochlea's hair cells, sorted by pitch, send signals to the brain. Human hair cells never grow back.

cards.headline: Every sound you hear ends as a ripple in a snail-shaped tube of fluid.
cards.body: A voice, a song, a dog barking: each arrives as sound waves in the air. Your ear's job is to turn them into electrical signals your brain can read. It takes a relay from air to bone to liquid.

cards.headline: Drum, bones, fluid
cards.body: Sound waves travel down your ear canal to the eardrum, which vibrates. It hands the vibrations to three tiny bones in the middle ear: the malleus, the incus and the stapes, a stirrup-shaped bone that is the smallest of the three. The bones amplify the vibrations and pass them into the cochlea, a snail-shaped, fluid-filled structure in the inner ear. Air, then bone, then liquid.

mascot.line: Think of a piano keyboard rolled up like a snail shell, with hair cells for keys.

cards.headline: Hair cells ride the wave
cards.body: Inside the cochlea, the vibrations start a traveling wave along a membrane, and sensory hair cells ride it. Cells near the wide end respond to high pitches, like a baby crying; those toward the center respond to low ones, like a big dog barking. As the cells move, tiny bristles on top bend, channels open and an electrical signal is born. The auditory nerve carries it to your brain.

cards.fact: Your hair cells are not on the replacement list.
cards.context: Unlike the hair cells of birds and amphibians, human hair cells don't grow back, and their damage and death cause most noise-induced hearing loss. Compare Level 10, where about 330 billion of your cells are replaced every day. The ones you hear with have to last.

title: Balance
objective: After this level you can explain how the inner ear keeps you balanced.
summary: Three fluid-filled canals in the inner ear sense head turns; tiny grains in two pouches feel gravity. When ears and eyes disagree, you get dizziness or motion sickness.

cards.headline: Spin in circles, stop, and the room keeps turning.
cards.body: You've stopped. Your eyes can see you've stopped. Something inside your head disagrees. That something is Level 61's missing sense, balance, and it lives right next door to your hearing.

cards.headline: Three loops of fluid
cards.body: Your balance organ, the vestibular system, is a maze of bone and soft tissue in your inner ear. It holds three fluid-filled semicircular canals, looped at roughly right angles to each other. When you turn your head, the fluid moves and bends hair cells, the same kind of sensor you hear with, which tells your brain which way you turned. Nod, shake or tilt, and the fluid reports it.

mascot.line: Pebbles in your ears, doing precision work. Nature has a sense of humor.

cards.headline: Tiny stones that feel gravity
cards.body: Two small pouches, the utricle and the saccule, sense which way is down. Their hair cells sit under a gel holding tiny grains of calcium carbonate. Gravity pulls on the grains and bends the hair cells, telling your brain if you're upright, leaning back or lying down. You carry a built-in spirit level, and it runs on tiny stones.

cards.headline: When the reports disagree
cards.body: Your brain builds balance from your eyes, your inner ears and the muscles and touch sensors in your legs. After spinning, canal fluid keeps moving though you've stopped: ears say motion, eyes say still, and you feel dizzy. Below deck on a ship it flips. Your inner ear feels the motion, your eyes see a still cabin, and that clash is the leading explanation for motion sickness.

title: Smell and Taste
objective: After this level you can explain how smell and taste work together to make flavor.
summary: Taste buds detect at least five tastes, and every taste area senses all of them. Flavor adds smell, reaching the nose from the throat as you chew, plus heat, cold and texture.

cards.headline: Your tongue can tell sweet from bitter. It can't tell a pear from an apple.
cards.body: That job needs your nose. When a cold blocks it, food tastes bland even though your tongue is fine. Flavor is a team effort, and the tongue isn't the star you think it is.

cards.headline: Five tastes, everywhere
cards.body: Taste cells sit in taste buds on your tongue, on the roof of your mouth and along your throat. They respond to at least five basic tastes: sweet, sour, bitter, salty and umami, the savory taste of glutamate in foods like broth, meat extracts and some cheeses. That's the whole menu your tongue can read. Everything else on your plate is reaching you another way.

mascot.line: Decades of classroom posters, all from one overdrawn graph. Science corrects itself, eventually.

cards.fact: The 'tongue map' is a myth.
cards.context: You may have seen a diagram with sweet at the tip and bitter at the back. In fact, taste cells for different tastes are scattered across the tongue, and every area with taste buds senses all the tastes. The map grew from a 1901 study that found only tiny differences in sensitivity, redrawn in the 1940s by Harvard psychologist Edwin Boring and read as separate zones.

cards.headline: The nose does the heavy lifting
cards.body: Smell comes from sensory cells high inside your nose. Odors reach them two ways: through your nostrils and, as you chew, up a channel from the roof of your throat to your nose. Your brain blends those smells with the basic tastes, plus heat, cold and texture, into flavor. That's what tells a pear from an apple, and why a blocked nose leaves food flat.

title: Touch and Pain
objective: After this level you can explain how the skin senses touch, heat and pain.
summary: Skin sensors for touch, temperature, pain and chemicals crowd the fingertips. Chili and menthol led to the heat and cold sensors (2021 Nobel). Pain is a vital warning.

cards.headline: A chili pepper tricks a heat sensor in your mouth.
cards.body: The burn comes from a chemical, not a flame. Working out how it fools you earned a share of the 2021 Nobel Prize, and it shows how your skin turns touch, warmth and pain into signals.

cards.headline: Four families of sensor
cards.body: Your skin's sensors come in four families: for touch and pressure, for temperature, for pain and for chemicals. The most common, free nerve endings, respond to pain, hot and cold, and light touch. Touch sensors crowd your fingertips and lips and thin out on hairy skin like your arms, legs and torso. That's why you test a fabric with your fingertips, not your elbow.

mascot.line: Chili plays the heat sensor and mint plays the cold one. Your nerves fall for it every time.

cards.headline: A chili, a mint and a Nobel Prize
cards.body: In the late 1990s, David Julius used capsaicin, the chemical that makes chilies burn, to find TRPV1, a sensor in nerve endings that switches on at painfully hot temperatures. Capsaicin flips the same switch. Julius and Ardem Patapoutian each used menthol to find a cold sensor, and Patapoutian found Piezo2, essential for touch and for Level 61's sense of body position. They shared the 2021 Nobel Prize.

cards.fact: Pain is a warning light, and life without it is dangerous.
cards.context: Pain helps you avoid danger and injury. People born with a rare condition called congenital insensitivity to pain never feel it when they're hurt. They can tell hot from cold, but not that a drink is burning their tongue, so they suffer more injuries and may live shorter lives. One form comes from changes in a single gene, SCN9A.

title: Optical Illusions
objective: After this level you can explain why the brain can be fooled by optical illusions.
summary: An optical illusion is a perception that contradicts reality. The Müller-Lyer lines and Adelson's checker-shadow squares show the brain's interpretations misfiring.

cards.headline: Two lines, exactly the same length. One looks longer.
cards.body: Add arrowheads to one line and outward-flaring fins to the other, and the fins win. Your eyes aren't broken. Your brain is interpreting what it sees, and here the interpretation goes wrong.

cards.headline: Seeing isn't measuring
cards.body: An optical illusion is a perception that contradicts reality. Some illusions come from light or poor lighting, some from the eye itself, and many from how your brain processes what the eyes send. The two lines are the Müller-Lyer illusion, published in 1889 by Franz Carl Müller-Lyer: equal lines, but the one with fins flaring outward looks longer. What you see is your brain's reading of the scene, not a ruler's.

mascot.line: Your brain subtracts a shadow that was never really there. Very diligent. Slightly wrong.

cards.headline: The shadow that fools you
cards.body: In Edward Adelson's 1995 checker-shadow illusion, a cylinder casts a shadow across a checkerboard. A square inside the shadow looks much lighter than one outside it, yet they're the exact same grey. Your visual system estimates where the light comes from and judges each surface's own shade, correcting for shadow. On a flat picture that correction misleads you. In the real world, it keeps a white shirt looking white in the shade.

cards.headline: You've been edited all along
cards.body: You've met this editor before. In Level 62 your brain turned the upside-down image on your retina upright, and quietly filled in each eye's blind spot. Illusions aren't a glitch in an otherwise perfect camera. They're the rare moments you catch your brain at work.

title: Checkpoint: The Senses
objective: After this level you can explain how the senses gather information and how the brain makes sense of it.
summary: Every sense turns a stimulus into a nerve signal (transduction). Sensation detects; perception interprets. And the brain tunes out what doesn't change: sensory adaptation.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 finale: you couldn't feel your socks until you read this.
cards.body: Your senses report all day long, yet you don't notice most of it. First, the one trick every sense shares. Then, why your brain stops listening to whatever doesn't change.

cards.headline: Every sense, one trick
cards.body: Every sense starts with specialized receptor cells that turn one kind of stimulus into a nerve signal, a step called transduction. In your retina, photoreceptors do it with light. In your cochlea, hair cells do it with vibration. Taste cells, the smell cells high in your nose and the sensors in your skin do it with chemicals, pressure and heat. Different doors, one currency.

cards.headline: Sensing isn't perceiving
cards.body: Sensation is a receptor detecting something. Perception is your brain organizing and interpreting it into an experience. They aren't the same: Level 69's checkerboard sent your eyes two identical greys, and your brain perceived two different ones. Your receptors collect the data. Your brain writes the story.

mascot.line: Your brain only reads the headlines. Steady things never make the front page.

cards.fact: You stop noticing what doesn't change.
cards.context: It's called sensory adaptation: we often stop perceiving stimuli that stay the same for a long time. Picture a hotel room with a light flashing steadily outside the window. After a while, you stop noticing it. Your socks are still there too. They've just stopped being news.

title: Skin
objective: After this level you can explain how skin protects the body.
summary: Skin, your largest organ, is topped by dead keratin-packed cells replaced about every 4 weeks. Its cool, dry, acidic surface, oil and friendly microbes keep germs out.

cards.headline: Your biggest organ is the one you're wearing.
cards.body: Skin is the largest organ in your body, and it covers every bit of you. It's also the first wall every germ runs into. So how does something this thin keep the outside world outside?

cards.headline: Three layers, one wall
cards.body: Skin is built in three layers. The deepest, the hypodermis, is mostly fat. Above it, the dermis holds blood vessels, hair follicles and sweat glands. On top sits the epidermis, made of closely packed epithelial cells: the covering tissue from Level 4. Laid out flat, an adult's skin covers about 1.8 square meters, roughly the top of a single bed.

mascot.line: Every handshake you have ever had was with dead cells. Friendly dead cells, though.

cards.headline: A wall built from dead bricks
cards.body: The very top of the epidermis is a layer of dry, dead cells packed with keratin, the tough, water-resistant protein in your hair and nails. That layer helps keep microbes out and water in. New cells are made at the bottom of the epidermis and pushed upward, dying as they go, and the whole outer layer is replaced about every 4 weeks.

cards.headline: Sour, dry and already occupied
cards.body: The surface is hostile ground for germs, too. It's cool, dry and slightly acidic, and that acid holds back harmful bacteria. Oil from glands in your skin kills bacteria as well. And the best spots are already taken: part of the microbiome from Level 8 lives on your skin, and those friendly microbes help protect you against more harmful ones. Germs arrive to find a moat and no vacancies.

title: Germs

summary: Germs cause infectious disease. Bacteria are single cells, mostly harmless; fungi include molds and yeasts; viruses are not cells and multiply only inside living cells.

cards.headline: 'Germ' isn't a species. It's a job title.
cards.body: Germs are the microbes behind infectious diseases, and the word covers very different things. The main kinds are bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites. Meet the first three, because telling them apart changes how you fight them.

Most viruses measure from about 20 to a few hundred nanometers, and none can multiply outside a living cell. A virus is a set of instructions looking for a factory.

cards.headline: Why telling them apart matters
cards.body: Built differently, fought differently. Antibiotics treat bacterial infections, but they don't work on viruses; for most viral infections, your immune system does the fighting. And 'kill every germ' was never the goal, because most bacteria don't make you sick. Some are downright useful, like the gut microbes from Level 8 that help break down your food.

title: The Immune System
objective: After this level you can explain how white blood cells fight infection.
summary: Innate immunity includes skin and phagocytes, found by Metchnikoff in 1882. Acquired immunity uses B cells that make antibodies, T cells, and memory.

cards.headline: In 1882, a zoologist stuck splinters into see-through starfish larvae.
cards.body: Elie Metchnikoff was studying the tiny animals in Messina, Italy. What he saw crowding around those splinters became one of the first clues to how your own body fights infection.

cards.headline: The devouring cells
cards.body: Certain cells in the larvae surrounded the splinters and engulfed them. Metchnikoff named them phagocytes, from Greek words meaning 'devouring cells', and the discovery earned him a share of the 1908 Nobel Prize. You have phagocytes too: white blood cells that swallow germs and dead or damaged cells. Your body runs its own cleanup crew, and it eats on the job.

cards.headline: The defenses you were born with
cards.body: Phagocytes belong to your innate immunity, the defense system you're born with. It's nonspecific: it doesn't need to know which germ it's facing. It also includes barriers like the skin from Level 71, which keeps harmful material out in the first place. Think of a wall with guards who throw out anything that doesn't belong.

mascot.line: Your immune system keeps a file on every germ it has beaten. Quietly, thoroughly, forever-ish.

cards.headline: Specialists who learn and remember
cards.body: Your second defense, acquired immunity, develops as you meet germs. It relies on lymphocytes, white blood cells of two kinds. B cells become plasma cells that make antibodies: proteins that lock onto one specific antigen, usually a protein on a germ's surface, and make it easier to destroy. T cells attack directly and help run the response. Afterwards, some B and T cells stay on as memory, so the next time that germ turns up, the answer comes faster.

title: Fever
objective: After this level you can explain why the body raises its temperature when it is sick.
summary: In a fever, pyrogens make the hypothalamus raise its temperature setting. The heat stirs white blood cells and slows some germs, a defense over 600 million years old.

cards.headline: When you're sick, your body turns up its own thermostat on purpose.
cards.body: A fever isn't your body overheating by accident. It's a new setting chosen by your brain. So why would the body make itself hotter, and why do you shiver while it does?

cards.headline: The thermostat in your brain
cards.body: In Level 1, your muscles and circulation shared the job of keeping you warm. The target they aim for is set by the hypothalamus, the part of the brain that regulates body temperature. During an infection, chemicals called pyrogens travel in the blood to the brain and push that setting up. Same team, new target.

cards.headline: Why you shiver while you're hot
cards.body: When the setting jumps, your real temperature is suddenly below the target, so you feel chilly and may even get shaking chills while your temperature climbs. When the fever breaks, it runs the other way: you feel warm, your skin flushes and you sweat. As Level 7 showed, evaporating sweat cools the skin. Freezing while burning up isn't a contradiction. It's catching up.

cards.headline: Heat as a weapon
cards.body: Why bother? Higher temperatures stimulate white blood cells, like the phagocytes in Level 73, to move, work and multiply, and they increase antibody production. Heat may also kill or slow the growth of some bacteria and viruses. It isn't cheap: each 1°C rise needs 10 to 12.5 percent more energy. Your body pays that bill because the fight is worth it.

mascot.line: A lizard with a fever goes and sits in the sun. Honestly, that sounds like a fair plan.

cards.fact: Even cold-blooded lizards run a fever.
cards.context: Fever has been part of fighting infection in warm- and cold-blooded animals for over 600 million years. Desert iguanas can't heat themselves from inside, so when they're infected they move somewhere warmer. In experiments, iguanas kept from warming up by about 2°C saw their survival fall by 75 percent.

title: Vaccines
objective: After this level you can explain how vaccines train the immune system.
summary: A vaccine imitates an infection so the body makes antibodies and memory without the disease. Vaccines are very safe and have saved at least 154 million lives since 1974.

cards.headline: A vaccine lets your immune system practice without the disease.
cards.body: Remember Level 73's memory cells, the reason a second meeting with a germ goes faster? A vaccine arranges the first meeting in advance, on your terms, without you getting sick.

cards.headline: A wanted poster, not the criminal
cards.body: A vaccine works by imitating an infection. Inside is an antigen: a killed or weakened form of the germ, a part of it, or genetic instructions (RNA or DNA) that tell your cells to make that part. Your immune system recognizes it, makes antibodies and remembers how to fight it. It learns the germ's face without meeting the germ at full strength.

cards.headline: Protection that stays
cards.body: After one or more doses, protection typically lasts years, decades or even a lifetime. If the real germ turns up, your trained defenses destroy it quickly. That's why a vaccinated person is far less likely to die or become seriously ill than someone whose immune system is unprepared.

mascot.line: A small sting in the arm, and your immune system gets the whole training manual.

cards.headline: Tested, watched and shared
cards.body: Vaccines are very safe. Each one passes several phases of clinical trials before it's used, and health authorities keep monitoring it afterwards. Side effects are usually minor and short, like a sore arm, and serious reactions are extremely rare. Vaccines protect other people too: those who can't be vaccinated, such as very young babies, depend on the people around them being vaccinated.

cards.fact: Vaccines have saved at least 154 million lives in 50 years.
cards.context: That's the estimate from a 2024 WHO-led study of immunization since 1974: about 6 lives every minute, 101 million of them infants. It found immunization to be the single greatest contribution of any health intervention to babies surviving into healthy adulthood.

title: Jenner and Smallpox
objective: After this level you can explain how Edward Jenner's cowpox experiment led to the first vaccine.
summary: Variolation was safer than smallpox but still risky. In 1796 Jenner showed cowpox protected against smallpox and named it vaccination. Smallpox was eradicated by 1980.

cards.headline: For centuries, the best defense against smallpox was catching it on purpose.
cards.body: Smallpox killed up to about 3 in 10 of the people who caught it. The protection people used was itself a gamble. Then Edward Jenner followed up a clue from the milkmaids.

cards.headline: Variolation: a smaller dose of danger
cards.body: Long before vaccines, people in Africa, India and China practiced variolation: material from a smallpox sore was scratched into a healthy person's arm, or breathed in. About 2 to 3 percent of them died, far fewer than from smallpox caught naturally. In 1721, Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, who had seen it in the Ottoman Empire, had her daughter variolated in London. Safer, yes. Safe, no.

cards.headline: The milkmaid clue
cards.body: Jenner noticed that milkmaids who had caught cowpox, a disease picked up from cows, didn't catch smallpox. On May 14, 1796, he took material from cowpox sores on the hand of a dairymaid, Sarah Nelmes, and inoculated 8-year-old James Phipps. In July he inoculated the boy with smallpox matter. No disease developed.

mascot.line: Somewhere in history there is a cow who never got the credit she deserved.

cards.headline: Named after a cow
cards.body: Jenner wasn't the first to use cowpox; a farmer, Benjamin Jesty, had done it earlier. But Jenner tested it and published his results in 1798, and he called the method vaccination, from the Latin vacca, 'cow'. Every vaccine in Level 75 still carries that cow in its name.

cards.fact: In 1980, WHO declared smallpox eradicated.
cards.context: It's the only human infectious disease ever eradicated. The last natural case was in Somalia in 1977, less than two centuries after James Phipps's cowpox.

title: Fleming and Penicillin
objective: After this level you can explain how Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin.
summary: In 1928 Fleming saw a mold stop bacteria and named its substance penicillin. Florey and Chain's Oxford team made it a medicine; all three shared the 1945 Nobel Prize.

cards.headline: Penicillin was discovered in 1928. Its first patient came in 1941.
cards.body: The famous part is a moldy dish and a lucky accident. The less famous part took a team in Oxford, a lot of glassware and even hospital bedpans. Both halves made the medicine.

cards.headline: The dish on the bench
cards.body: Before a two-week vacation, Alexander Fleming left a dish of Staphylococcus bacteria on his lab bench. A Penicillium mold spore got in, perhaps through a window, more likely floating up a stairwell from the lab below. In September 1928, Fleming saw that the bacteria failed to grow near the mold. Something the mold made was killing them, and he named it penicillin.

cards.headline: A discovery isn't a medicine
cards.body: Fleming published in 1929, and the scientific community took little notice. Working with two young researchers, he also failed to stabilize and purify penicillin, let alone make enough to test on patients. A dish that kills bacteria is a clue. A medicine is something you can make, measure and give.

mascot.line: Recycling medicine from a patient's urine. That is how short the supply really was.

cards.headline: Oxford turns mold into medicine
cards.body: In the late 1930s, Howard Florey and Ernst Chain's team at Oxford isolated and purified penicillin, growing the mold in any vessel they could find, hospital bedpans included. In 1940, four infected mice given penicillin were alive hours later; four untreated mice were dead. In February 1941 a policeman became the first patient. He improved, then died when the supply ran out, even though they recovered penicillin from his urine.

cards.fact: Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel Prize.
cards.context: By then, a British-American wartime effort of thousands of people and some 35 institutions was producing penicillin. It works by blocking the enzymes bacteria use to build their cell walls. The accident gave the clue; the teamwork gave the cure.

title: Handwashing
objective: After this level you can explain why handwashing saves lives, from Semmelweis to today.
summary: In 1847 Semmelweis cut childbed fever deaths from about 18 to 1 percent with handwashing, and was rejected. Today the CDC calls soap and water the best way to remove germs.

cards.headline: In 1847, one doctor cut deaths on a ward from about 18 to about 1 percent.
cards.body: His treatment wasn't a drug. He made medical students wash their hands in a chlorinated lime solution. Most of his colleagues rejected the idea anyway.

cards.headline: Two divisions, two death rates
cards.body: Ignaz Semmelweis worked in a maternity clinic in Vienna with two divisions: medical students trained in one, midwives in the other. In the students' division, deaths from childbed fever were two or three times higher. Same hospital, same illness, very different odds. The question was what the students were bringing with them.

mascot.line: Right answer, wrong decade. Sometimes the data has to wait for the world to catch up.

cards.headline: The clue from the dissecting room
cards.body: Then a colleague died of a wound infection picked up while examining the body of a woman who had died of childbed fever. Semmelweis reasoned that students coming straight from the dissecting room carried the infection on their hands. In 1847 he ordered them to wash in chlorinated lime before each examination, and deaths fell from about 18 percent to about 1 percent. The weight of medical authority still stood against him.

cards.headline: What the CDC says today
cards.body: The CDC says washing with soap and water is the best way to get rid of germs in most situations. Scrub for at least 20 seconds, about two runs of 'Happy Birthday'. Lathering and scrubbing create friction that lifts dirt, grease and microbes off your skin. It matters because hands carry germs to your eyes, nose and mouth, right past Level 71's wall.

cards.fact: Handwashing cuts diarrheal illness by 23 to 40 percent.
cards.context: That's the CDC's summary of the research. Handwashing also cuts respiratory illnesses, such as colds, by 16 to 21 percent. Semmelweis's basin of chlorinated lime was the right idea after all.

title: Allergies
objective: After this level you can explain what an allergy is and why some people have them.
summary: An allergy is an immune false alarm: IgE antibodies prime mast cells, which release histamine on a later exposure. Genes and environment both play a part.

cards.headline: An allergy is your immune system sounding the alarm over pollen.
cards.body: Normally your immune system fights germs. In most allergic reactions, it's responding to a false alarm: something that doesn't bother most other people. So what goes wrong, and why only in some of us?

cards.headline: The usual suspects
cards.body: The triggers are called allergens. Common ones include pollen, dust mites, mold spores, pet dander, foods, insect stings and some medicines. None of them is a germ trying to infect you. Your defenses have simply locked onto the wrong target, like a smoke alarm going off over toast.

mascot.line: Same antibody machinery that fights real germs, aimed at a flower. Enthusiastic, just misdirected.

cards.headline: Loaded first, triggered later
cards.body: Allergies run on a kind of antibody called IgE. Once the immune system has made IgE against an allergen, those antibodies attach to mast cells and wait. That's called sensitization. The next time the allergen arrives, it binds to the IgE, and the mast cells release histamine, the chemical behind symptoms like a runny nose and swelling. The first meeting loads the trap; a later one springs it.

cards.headline: Why you, and not your friend
cards.body: Genes and environment both play a role. If both your parents have allergies, there's a good chance you'll have them too. Allergies are common: in 2021, 31.8 percent of US adults had a diagnosed seasonal allergy, eczema or food allergy. Most reactions are a nuisance, but a severe one, called anaphylaxis, can be life-threatening.

title: Checkpoint: Defending the Body
objective: After this level you can explain how skin, the immune system and medicine protect us from germs.
summary: Defenses in layers: the skin wall, innate phagocytes and fever, acquired immunity with memory, and human tools. Lymph nodes are where white blood cells fight germs.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 finale: your defenses are built like a castle.
cards.body: A wall, guards on patrol and specialists who remember every enemy, plus a few tools humans added. First, a walk along the walls. Then a stop at the barracks you can sometimes feel swelling in your neck.

cards.headline: Four layers of defense
cards.body: Layer one is the wall: dead, keratin-packed skin cells, replaced about every 4 weeks, on a dry, acidic surface. Layer two is innate immunity, the defense you're born with: phagocytes devour intruders, and fever's heat stirs white blood cells on. Layer three is acquired immunity: B cells, T cells and memory. Layer four is ours. Soap and water scrub germs away, vaccines train memory in advance, and penicillin blocks bacteria from building their cell walls.

cards.fact: Your 'swollen glands' are your immune system at work.
cards.context: Those glands are lymph nodes, part of the lymphatic system from Level 1 that returns fluid and defends against germs. They sit along lymph vessels in places like your neck, armpits and groin. Along with the spleen, they're where white blood cells fight infection, and infections are the most common reason they swell.

title: From One Cell to a Baby
objective: After this level you can explain how a baby develops from a single cell.
summary: Egg and sperm, 23 chromosomes each, fuse into one cell with 46. It divides, its cells specialize, it becomes a fetus at week 10, and birth comes at about 40 weeks.

cards.headline: Every person you've ever met started as one cell.
cards.body: So did you. That first cell had no heart, no brain and no bones, just a full set of instructions. About 40 weeks later, there was a baby. Here's how one cell pulls that off.

cards.headline: Half a set from each side
cards.body: It begins with fertilization: a sperm cell and an egg cell fuse into one new cell, the zygote. Each of those two cells carries exactly 23 chromosomes, one of each pair. Together they make 46. Remember Level 5's 23 pairs? This is where they come from: in every pair, one chromosome is from each parent.

mascot.line: One cell, one instruction book, and somehow it builds a whole person. No foreman required.

cards.headline: One cell, many careers
cards.body: In its first days the zygote divides, then divides again, into a ball of cells. Then the copies start to specialize, step by step, into every cell type the body needs: nerve cells, muscle cells, liver cells, about 400 kinds in all. Each keeps the same DNA. Same instruction book, very different careers.

title: Inherited Traits
objective: After this level you can explain how children inherit traits from both parents.
summary: You get two versions of each gene, one from each parent, and a dominant one can mask the other. But most traits, even eye color, involve many genes, and every egg or sperm carries a new mix.

cards.headline: Half your DNA came from each parent. You're still not an even blend.
cards.body: Brothers and sisters share the same two parents, yet each gets a different mix. Each parent can make over eight million different eggs or sperm. So how do traits actually pass down? It starts with pairs.

cards.headline: Two copies of almost everything
cards.body: Your 46 chromosomes come as 23 pairs, so wherever DNA varies between people, you carry two versions, called alleles: one from each parent. For some traits, one allele is dominant: a single copy is enough to show, and it masks the other, recessive one. Genes come in pairs, like shoes, one from each parent's closet.

mascot.line: Brown beats blue was a tidy story. Your eyes prefer the messy truth.

cards.headline: Eye color is not a coin toss
cards.body: Researchers used to think eye color was one gene, with brown dominant over blue. It's more complex. The color comes from how much melanin pigment sits in your iris, and several genes, led by two called OCA2 and HERC2, combine to set it, giving a continuum of shades. So, although it's uncommon, two blue-eyed parents can have a brown-eyed child.

cards.fact: Many traits are team efforts.
cards.context: Traits like height and skin color are polygenic: two or more genes shape them, and the environment usually has a say too. Remember Level 6? Height involves hundreds of gene variants, each with a small effect, plus things like nutrition.

cards.headline: Why siblings differ
cards.body: Each egg or sperm gets one chromosome from each of a parent's 23 pairs, sorted at random. That alone allows over eight million different combinations, and paired chromosomes also swap matching pieces first. So no two eggs or sperm are likely to match, and siblings each get their own shuffle of the same two decks.

title: Growing Up
objective: After this level you can explain how growth spurts and hormones change the body.
summary: A hormone relay from hypothalamus to pituitary to ovaries or testes starts puberty. Growth spurts peak around 11.5 (girls) and 13.5 (boys); the brain matures last.

cards.headline: Puberty starts in the brain, not the body.
cards.body: Before anything visible changes, a small part of your brain starts sending chemical messages. Here's the relay that turns a child's body into an adult's, and why the finish line comes much later than you'd guess.

cards.headline: A three-step hormone relay
cards.body: The trigger is the hypothalamus, a small part of the brain. It releases a hormone called GnRH, which tells the pituitary, a pea-sized gland just below it, to send out two more hormones, LH and FSH. Those reach the ovaries or testes, which start releasing sex hormones such as estrogens and testosterone. Those hormones drive the changes you can see. Brain, gland, organs: a relay race run in chemicals.

cards.headline: A wide starting window
cards.body: Puberty is the time of life when the body matures sexually. Its physical changes typically begin between ages 8 and 13 in girls and between 9 and 14 in boys. That's a window of about five years, so two friends of the same age can be at very different stages. The relay starts when it starts.

cards.fact: Girls' growth spurt peaks around age 11.5; boys' around 13.5.
cards.context: Girls' growth then slows around 16, and boys' around 18. New body hair appears too, usually at about 9 or 10 in girls and about 12 in boys. That's why girls often shoot up first, and boys catch up later.

mascot.line: Next time someone says you're not thinking ahead, you can blame the construction schedule.

cards.headline: The brain signs off last
cards.body: Your brain stops growing in size by early adolescence, but it keeps fine-tuning how it works until the mid-to-late 20s. One of the last parts to mature is the prefrontal cortex, just behind your forehead, which handles planning and decisions. Growing up happens in stages, and the planning department finishes last.

title: Why We Age
objective: After this level you can explain what happens to cells as we get older.
summary: Normal cells divide only about 40 to 60 times, as telomeres shorten with each division. Senescent cells that stop dividing but linger spread inflammation, and damage builds up over time.

cards.headline: Your cells can only divide so many times.
cards.body: Scientists once believed cells grown in a dish could divide forever. In 1961 two researchers showed they can't, and that limit became one of the first clues to why bodies age.

cards.headline: The Hayflick limit
cards.body: In 1961 Leonard Hayflick and Paul Moorhead reported that normal human cells grown in a dish divide only about 40 to 60 times, then stop. That overturned the claim, made by Alexis Carrel, that cultured cells could keep dividing forever. The cap became known as the Hayflick limit, and Hayflick linked it to aging.

cards.headline: A fuse on every chromosome
cards.body: Why the cap? Each chromosome ends in a telomere, a stretch of repeated DNA letters. Every time a cell divides, some of those repeats get cut off. Eventually the telomeres are too short for the cell to divide successfully. Remember Level 10's 330 billion cells replaced every day? Each division burns a little more fuse.

mascot.line: Retired, but still sending grumpy memos to the neighbors. We've all met a cell like that.

cards.headline: Cells that won't leave
cards.body: A cell that stops dividing but doesn't die is called senescent. Senescent cells never divide again, and they build up in almost all tissues as we age. Worse, they release harmful molecules that trigger inflammation and disrupt the cells around them, like a rotten apple spoiling the barrel. Researchers link them to many illnesses of aging.

cards.fact: Aging is damage adding up.
cards.context: The WHO describes biological aging as the result of many kinds of molecular and cellular damage building up over time. Those changes are only loosely tied to age in years, which is why two people with the same birthday can age very differently.

title: How Long Humans Live
objective: After this level you can explain why life expectancy has risen so much.
summary: Global life expectancy reached 73.3 years in 2024 (UN). Past averages were dragged down by child deaths; gains now reach every age. Jeanne Calment lived to 122.

cards.headline: Life expectancy is an average. Averages can hide a lot.
cards.body: Life expectancy is the number of years people can expect to live, on average. Today the world's stands at 73.3 years. To see why it used to be so much lower, you have to look at who was dying.

cards.fact: Global life expectancy at birth reached 73.3 years in 2024.
cards.context: That's 8.4 years longer than in 1995, according to the UN's World Population Prospects 2024. It dipped during the COVID-19 pandemic and has been rising again since.

cards.headline: The average that fooled everyone
cards.body: Before modern times, about a quarter of babies died in their first year, and almost half of children died before the end of puberty. Deaths that early drag an average down hard. So a low life expectancy never meant adults routinely died young; it meant many people never got to be adults.

cards.headline: Then every age gained
cards.body: Saving children was a huge part of the rise, but not all of it: life expectancy has increased at every age. Better nutrition and sanitation, fighting infection and modern health care all played a part. Aging itself hasn't gone away (Level 85's damage still builds up); more people simply live long enough to experience it.

mascot.line: Even a record-holder gets fact-checked. Good science double-checks everyone, however old.

cards.fact: The oldest verified person lived to 122.
cards.context: Jeanne Calment of France died in 1997, aged 122 years and 164 days. In 2018 researchers claimed her daughter had taken her identity decades earlier. The scientists who validated her age rejected the claim, and most researchers still accept the record.

title: Our Ancestors in Us
objective: After this level you can explain which features our bodies inherited from early humans.
summary: Walking upright goes back about 6 million years, big brains came later, and Homo sapiens arose in Africa about 300,000 years ago. Many people also carry 1 to 4 percent Neanderthal DNA.

cards.headline: The design of your lower back is millions of years old.
cards.body: Our species appeared in Africa about 300,000 years ago, but many of your body's features are far older, inherited from earlier humans. Read your body like a family history, starting with the way you stand.

cards.headline: Standing up came first
cards.body: Walking on two legs is the oldest of these inheritances: the oldest evidence for it comes from fossils of the earliest known humans, about 6 million years ago. The curve of your lower back, which absorbs shock with every step, is uniquely human, and a similar curve shows up in the spine of an early human called Australopithecus africanus.

cards.headline: Then the brain grew
cards.body: Big brains came much later. The earliest humans had brains about the size of a chimpanzee's. Over human evolution, brain size tripled, growing fastest during a time of dramatic climate change. Our own species, Homo sapiens, evolved in Africa about 300,000 years ago, carrying that big brain on top of a very old way of walking.

mascot.line: Some of your ancestors' relatives were Neanderthals. Family reunions used to be very interesting.

cards.fact: Many people carry some Neanderthal DNA.
cards.context: Svante Pääbo's team published the first Neanderthal genome in 2010 and showed that our species interbred with Neanderthals. For people of European or Asian descent, about 1 to 4 percent of their DNA comes from them. The work won Pääbo the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

cards.headline: A family tree in bone and DNA
cards.body: Fossils and DNA tell the same story: humans are one of more than 200 species of primates, and Neanderthals are our closest extinct relatives. Your body is a patchwork of those inheritances: an upright walker's spine, a big brain, and, for many people, a little Neanderthal.

title: Leftovers of Evolution
objective: After this level you can explain body parts like the appendix and goosebumps.
summary: Vestigial parts are ancestral leftovers, like the goosebump muscle and the embryo's tail. Leftover isn't useless: the appendix may shelter gut bacteria.

cards.headline: You have muscles built to fluff up fur you don't have.
cards.body: Goosebumps are one of several body parts that make the most sense as leftovers from our ancestors. But leftover doesn't always mean useless, as your appendix is quietly proving.

cards.headline: What vestigial means
cards.body: Biologists call a structure vestigial when it has little or no apparent function and looks like a residual part from a past common ancestor. Wings on flightless birds and hind leg bones in whales are classic examples. They're one line of evidence for evolution, and your own body has a few.

mascot.line: A leftover with a side job. Evolution is not big on throwing things out.

cards.headline: Goosebumps
cards.body: Each hair has a small muscle, the arrector pili, that can make it stand up. On a furry animal, like a frightened cat, that traps a layer of insulating air. On us, with far less hair, you mostly just get bumps. Yet in 2020 Harvard researchers found, in mice, that the same muscle and nerve also help regulate the stem cells that grow new hair.

cards.headline: A tail, mostly gone
cards.body: Human embryos, like those of other great apes, have a tail that's lost before birth. What remains is your tailbone, or coccyx. It isn't idle, though: it anchors muscles, supports tendons and ligaments, and helps bear your weight when you sit, like one leg of a tripod.

cards.fact: The appendix: vestigial, but not useless.
cards.context: This small tube attached to the start of the large intestine has immune tissue and may shelter helpful gut bacteria that restock the gut after an illness. A 2017 study of 533 mammal species found the appendix evolved independently over 30 times. Remember Level 8's gut microbes, which help digest your food? This may be their backup.

title: The Body Clock
objective: After this level you can explain daily body rhythms and why jet lag happens.
summary: Circadian rhythms run on about 24 hours, set by light and led by the SCN, which controls melatonin. Jet lag is the clock lagging local time, catching up 1 to 1.5 hours a day.

cards.headline: Fly across an ocean and your body keeps the old time.
cards.body: Your phone switches time zones in a second. Your body can take days, because for a while your rhythms stay anchored to home time. There's a clock inside your brain, and it doesn't read the airline schedule.

cards.headline: A rhythm for almost everything
cards.body: Circadian rhythms are the physical, mental and behavioral changes your body goes through over a 24-hour cycle. Nearly every tissue and organ has its own, shaping sleep patterns, hormone release, appetite and digestion, and body temperature. Light and dark set them more than anything else.

cards.headline: The master clock
cards.body: Conducting them all is a master clock in the brain: a group of nerve cells called the suprachiasmatic nucleus, or SCN. It tracks how much light your eyes receive and controls the hormone melatonin. In the evening it has your brain make more melatonin, and you get sleepy. The clock's gears were uncovered in fruit flies, winning Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash and Michael Young the 2017 Nobel Prize.

mascot.line: Heading east? Your body clock would like a word, and several days to think about it.

cards.headline: Why jet lag happens
cards.body: Jet lag is a temporary mismatch between your body clock and local time. Your clock adapts only about 1 hour a day after flying east and about 1.5 hours a day after flying west. West is easier because the inner clock runs slightly longer than 24 hours, so staying up later comes more naturally than going to bed earlier. Daylight helps it catch up.

cards.fact: Teenage body clocks run late.
cards.context: In teens, melatonin stays high later at night and drops later in the morning than in children or adults. That may explain why so many teens stay up late and struggle to wake early. Blame the timing.

title: Checkpoint: Growing and Changing
objective: After this level you can explain how genes, hormones and time shape a body from birth to old age.
summary: One life, from zygote to senescent cells. And epigenetics: chemical tags that switch genes on or off without changing DNA, which is why identical twins drift apart as they age.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 finale: identical twins start the same and drift apart.
cards.body: Identical twins share the same DNA from their first cell. Yet as they age they grow more different, in ways that go deeper than fingerprints. First, one life at a glance. Then, the switches that time flips.

cards.headline: Switches on the DNA
cards.body: Your DNA letters stay the same for life, but your cells attach chemical tags to DNA that turn genes on or off. That's epigenetics. A common tag is a methyl group: when methyl groups sit on a gene, that gene is switched off. Diet and pollutants can change the tags, and cells keep them when they divide. Same text, different highlights.

mascot.line: Same genes, different lives, different switches. That's the whole chapter in one pair of twins.

cards.fact: Identical twins drift apart with age.
cards.context: A 2005 study found that young identical twins have nearly indistinguishable epigenetic tags, while older identical twins differ markedly. Add Level 83's fingerprints, shaped in the womb, and the lesson is clear: genes write the book, but life keeps editing the highlights.

title: A Balanced Diet
objective: After this level you can describe what a balanced diet looks like.
summary: WHO's healthy-diet guidance rests on four principles (adequacy, balance, moderation, diversity) plus a few numbers: 400 g of fruit and vegetables a day, and limits on free sugars and salt.

cards.headline: There's no single perfect plate. The WHO says so itself.
cards.body: Its healthy-diet guidance, updated in January 2026, says the exact mix differs with the person, the culture and the foods grown nearby. So what stays the same on every healthy plate, from Lagos to Lima?

cards.headline: Four words behind every healthy plate
cards.body: The WHO describes a healthy diet with four principles. Adequacy: enough of the nutrients your body needs, without going over. Balance: the energy you take in matches the energy you use. Moderation: going easy on things that can harm in large amounts. Diversity: a wide variety of foods, within and across food groups. Get those right, the WHO says, and a diet helps protect against malnutrition and diseases such as diabetes, heart disease, stroke and cancer. Different kitchens, same four rules.

cards.fact: WHO recommends at least 400 g of fruit and vegetables a day for everyone over 10.
cards.context: That number is behind the NHS's famous '5 A Day': the NHS counts one portion as 80 g, and five portions make 400 g. Younger children get smaller targets from the WHO: at least 250 g at ages 2 to 5 and 350 g at ages 6 to 9. A slogan, it turns out, is just arithmetic.

mascot.line: An apple gets a pass. Apple juice doesn't. Same fruit, different rulebook.

cards.headline: Moderation has numbers too
cards.body: The WHO advises keeping free sugars under 10 percent of daily energy. Free sugars are those added by a manufacturer, cook or consumer, plus the sugars in honey, syrups and fruit juice; the sugar inside a fresh apple doesn't count. For salt, the limit is under 5 g a day, just under a teaspoon. The world averages about 11 g, more than double, and in many countries most of it arrives already inside processed foods like bread, cheese and salty snacks, not from the shaker.

title: Exercise
objective: After this level you can explain what exercise does for the heart, the muscles and the brain.
summary: WHO's 2020 guidelines: an average of 60 active minutes a day for ages 5 to 17, 150 to 300 a week for adults. Activity builds heart, lung, muscle and bone fitness and helps the brain.

cards.headline: About 4 in 5 teenagers worldwide don't move as much as the WHO recommends.

cards.headline: The talk test
cards.body: How hard is 'moderate'? The CDC has a shortcut: during moderate activity you can talk, but not sing. At vigorous intensity you can't say more than a few words without pausing for breath. And the WHO counts it all: walking, cycling, sports, active play, even getting around town. Its headline message is that any amount of activity is better than none. No gym membership required.

mascot.line: Every staircase is a tiny workout. Your heart, lungs and legs all clock in together.

cards.headline: What it does for heart, muscles and brain
cards.body: The WHO lists the payoffs. For children and teens: fitter heart, lungs and muscles, better heart and metabolic health, stronger bones, and better thinking and mental health. For adults: lower risk of heart disease, high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes, better sleep, and fewer symptoms of anxiety and depression. The CDC adds that some brain benefits show up right after a single session. Your brain gets paid on the day.

title: Sleep and Health
objective: After this level you can explain why sleep matters for health.
summary: CDC advice (from AASM): 9 to 12 hours of sleep at ages 6 to 12, 8 to 10 for teens, 7+ for adults. Sleep helps memory, growth, immunity and the heart.

cards.body: These numbers come from sleep scientists at the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, and they're not about laziness. The NIH says sleep helps you learn and form long-term memories, and in children and teens it supports growth and development. Short on sleep, people struggle to focus and think clearly. So an all-nighter before a test trades away the very thing that helps the studying stick.

mascot.line: Eight hours of doing nothing that is secretly doing everything.

cards.headline: A lighter shift for your heart
cards.body: The rest of the body cashes in too. During non-REM sleep your heart rate and blood pressure fall, so your heart doesn't work as hard. Some immune cells work harder while you sleep, and people who don't get enough may catch colds and other infections more easily. The CDC links enough sleep to lower risk of type 2 diabetes, heart disease, high blood pressure and stroke. Sleep is maintenance with the lights off.

title: Stress
objective: After this level you can explain how stress affects the body.
summary: Stress is a response to a demand. The amygdala alerts the hypothalamus, adrenaline and cortisol rev you up, and a brake calms you. Short bursts help; lasting stress harms.

cards.headline: Your body can treat a traffic jam like a threat to your life.
cards.body: Stress is your body's response to a demand, from a pile of homework to an illness. The alarm system behind it is fast, and not very good at telling a bear from a deadline. Here's how it works.

cards.headline: The alarm goes off before you know why
cards.body: When your eyes or ears pick up danger, the signal reaches the amygdala, which instantly alerts the hypothalamus, the command center for the response. This starts even before your brain's visual centers have fully worked out what you saw. That's why you can flinch at a shape in the dark before you realize it's only a coat.

cards.headline: Gas, then brake
cards.body: Next come hormones. Adrenaline makes your heart beat faster, pushing blood to your muscles, heart and other vital organs. Breathing speeds up, small airways in the lungs open wide, and stored sugar and fat are released for quick energy. As that surge fades, a second system keeps cortisol flowing to hold you on alert. When the threat passes, cortisol falls and the parasympathetic nervous system acts as the brake. Walter Cannon named this the fight-or-flight response in the early 1900s.

mascot.line: Even a good alarm needs someone to help find the off switch. That's what trusted people are for.

cards.headline: Useful in bursts, harmful on repeat
cards.body: A short burst of stress isn't all bad: it can push you to meet a deadline. The trouble is stress that doesn't let up. Long-lasting stress can disturb sleep and affect the immune, digestive and cardiovascular systems. Health guides from NIMH and KidsHealth say that when stress feels like too much or won't go away, talking with a trusted adult or a health professional can help. An alarm is useful. An alarm that never switches off isn't.
