title: Sun and Skin
objective: After this level you can explain how sunlight helps make vitamin D and how too much harms skin.
summary: Skin makes vitamin D from UVB in sunlight. Too much UV damages DNA and raises skin cancer risk; WHO advises protection at UV Index 3+, and the CDC advises SPF 15+ sunscreen.

cards.headline: The same sunshine helps build your bones and can burn your skin.
cards.body: The WHO calls small amounts of ultraviolet (UV) radiation essential to good health, because it leads to vitamin D. Too much does the opposite. The difference is the dose.

cards.headline: A vitamin your skin makes
cards.body: Your skin makes vitamin D when ultraviolet B (UVB) rays in sunlight reach it. Vitamin D helps control the calcium and phosphate that keep bones, teeth and muscles healthy; too little can lead to rickets in children. One catch: window glass blocks UVB. That sunny spot by the window warms you up, but it won't make any vitamin D.

cards.fact: In the UK, sunlight from October to early March can't make enough vitamin D.
cards.context: The NHS says skin there makes vitamin D from sunlight from about late March or early April to the end of September. For the darker months, UK government advice is that everyone consider a daily vitamin D supplement. Same sun, weaker deal.

cards.headline: Too much of a good thing
cards.body: The WHO lists DNA damage and sunburn as short-term effects of too much UV. Over the years, it raises the risk of skin cancer, cataracts in the eyes and early skin ageing, and sunburns in childhood raise skin cancer risk later in life. A tan isn't a badge of health either: the CDC calls any change in skin color after UV exposure, tan or burn, a sign of injury.

mascot.line: Shade, hat, sunglasses, sunscreen. Sunscreen is the last line, not the whole wall.

cards.headline: What the WHO and the CDC recommend
cards.body: The WHO recommends sun protection whenever the UV Index reaches 3 or above: shade, especially around midday, protective clothing, a wide-brimmed hat, sunglasses and broad-spectrum sunscreen. The CDC's sunscreen advice is SPF 15 or higher, reapplied after 2 hours and after swimming, sweating or toweling off. And the WHO adds one warning: sunscreen isn't a ticket to stay out longer.

title: Testing Medicines
objective: After this level you can explain how new medicines are tested before doctors use them.
summary: Medicines go from lab tests through Phases 1 to 3, then Phase 4 after approval. Placebos, random allocation and blinding separate a drug's real effect from chance and hope.

cards.headline: In 1948, sealed envelopes decided who got a new drug.
cards.body: Britain's Medical Research Council was testing streptomycin against tuberculosis. Doctors couldn't pick who got it: the choice came from random numbers hidden in sealed envelopes. It's widely regarded as the first randomized controlled trial. Why go to all that trouble?

cards.headline: The fake pill that keeps trials honest
cards.body: In many trials, one group gets the medicine and another gets a placebo: an inactive substance that looks just like it. Why? People can feel better simply because they expect a treatment to help. That's the placebo effect. Comparing the two groups shows whether changes come from the treatment or from chance. If the pill and the placebo do equally well, the pill isn't the one doing the work.

mascot.line: If nobody knows who got the real pill, nobody can nudge the answer. Clever, and a little sneaky.

cards.headline: Random and blind
cards.body: Back to 1948's envelopes. Allocating patients at random stops researchers from choosing, even unconsciously, who gets the new drug, a choice that could tilt the result. Blinding goes further. In a blind test, patients don't know whether they got the drug or the placebo; in a double-blind test, their doctors don't know either. Nobody's hopes get a vote.

title: Surgery Then and Now
objective: After this level you can explain how anesthesia and clean operating rooms changed surgery.
summary: In 1846 ether made surgery painless. From 1865 Joseph Lister fought wound infection with carbolic acid, and today's operating rooms aim for asepsis, down to the gloves.

cards.headline: 'Before whom in all time surgery was agony.'
cards.body: Those words are carved on the grave of William Morton, a Boston dentist. Two breakthroughs changed surgery for good: first taking away the pain, then keeping the germs out.

cards.headline: Ether Day, 1846
cards.body: On 16 October 1846, at Massachusetts General Hospital, Morton had a young housepainter named Edward Gilbert Abbott breathe ether while a surgeon removed a tumor from his neck. Abbott reported feeling no pain. Until then patients felt every cut, so surgeons had to work fast. Now they could slow down and be careful. The date became known as Ether Day.

cards.headline: Surviving the operation, not the wound
cards.body: Painless surgery still had a killer problem. In Joseph Lister's ward in Glasgow, 45 to 50 percent of amputation patients died of sepsis, an infection, between 1861 and 1865. After reading Louis Pasteur's germ theory, Lister concluded that microorganisms caused it, the same kind of tiny life Leeuwenhoek first spotted in Level 9. From 1865 he cleaned instruments and wounds with carbolic acid, and deaths in his ward fell sharply.

mascot.line: A kindness for one nurse's hands turned into protection for millions of patients. Not bad for a pair of gloves.

cards.headline: From killing germs to keeping them out
cards.body: Modern operating rooms aim for asepsis, freedom from disease-causing germs: everything that touches the surgical field is sterilized, typically by steam under pressure in an autoclave. Even the gloves have a story. In 1889 at Johns Hopkins, surgeon William Halsted had thin rubber gloves made for nurse Caroline Hampton, whose hands were damaged by harsh disinfectants. Made to protect her skin, gloves were later linked to fewer infections.

title: Organ Transplants
objective: After this level you can explain how organ transplants work and why matching matters.
summary: The immune system can reject a donated organ. The 1954 twin kidney transplant worked because twins match; blood and tissue matching plus immunosuppressants help everyone else.

cards.headline: Before a famous operation, two brothers were fingerprinted at a police station.
cards.body: Doctors needed proof that Richard and Ronald Herrick were truly identical twins, so they ran 17 tests. Why did being identical matter so much?

cards.headline: The body's ID check
cards.body: Your cells carry antigens, proteins on their surfaces. A donated organ carries someone else's, and the immune system can attack it. That's rejection. No two people have identical tissue antigens, except identical twins, whose tissues are genetically identical. That's why transplants between identical twins are almost never rejected. That's why the Herricks' 17 tests mattered so much.

cards.fact: On 23 December 1954, Richard Herrick received a kidney from his identical twin, Ronald.
cards.context: Joseph Murray's team in Boston performed the first successful human organ transplant. Murray had learned from grafting skin that tissue from an identical twin isn't rejected. Richard lived eight more years, and Murray later shared the 1990 Nobel Prize for his transplant work.

mascot.line: One donor, up to eight lives. That is teamwork on a whole new level.

cards.headline: Matching everyone else
cards.body: Most people don't have a twin to ask. So before a transplant, doctors check blood type and tissue type in donor and recipient; the closer the match, the lower the risk of rejection. Most recipients then take immunosuppressant medicines for life to hold off the attack. Those drugs let Murray's team transplant a kidney from an unrelated donor in 1962. Today one organ donor can save up to 8 lives, and a living person can give a kidney, since people can live with one.

cards.headline: The doctor who cracked one hand
cards.body: Does knuckle cracking cause arthritis? Donald Unger tested it on himself. For 50 years he cracked the knuckles of his left hand at least twice a day, leaving the right as a control. In 1998 he reported no arthritis in either hand, and won an Ig Nobel Prize for it in 2009. One man proves little, but a 2011 study of 215 people found hand arthritis about as common in crackers as in non-crackers.

mascot.line: Expectations are powerful. Even the grown-ups got a placebo effect of their own.

cards.headline: The sugar rush that wasn't there
cards.body: Double-blind trials find sugar doesn't change children's behavior or thinking. So why do parents see it? In a 1994 study, every boy got a sugar-free placebo, but some mothers were told their sons had been given sugar. Those mothers rated their sons as more hyperactive. The sugar rush was in the watching.
